PROP
39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 39
VOTER ID: A BIPARTISAN WAY TO INCREASE TRUST IN OUR ELECTIONS
Democratic, Independent, and Republican voters all agree on one thing: Voter ID is a common-sense reform to increase trust and participation in our elections. That’s why almost half the signatures to put Prop. 39 on the ballot came from Democratic and Independent voters and polls show widespread super-majority support across all political parties for Voter ID.
PROP. 39 KEEPS VOTING ACCESSIBLE AND GUARANTEES A FREE VOTER ID
Prop. 39 keeps mail ballots, extended polling hours and all other conveniences in place for voting accessibility.
Voters can use a variety of easily-obtained government IDs to vote—and this measure even guarantees every voter a FREE Voter ID if they want one.
California currently uses a slow process to check signatures on mail ballots that not only delays election results but also puts your vote at risk of not being counted if your signature is flagged as not matching. Many voters say they cannot always remember how they signed their name years ago when they first registered to vote. In the last election, more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches—and more than 200,000 voters endured hassles just to get their vote to count.
VOTER ID INCREASES PARTICIPATION
Voter ID does not suppress voting—in fact it increases voter participation. Every state with Voter ID laws and free identification for eligible voters that cannot afford or access identification, has seen an increase in voting. Suppression and lower turnout happen when voters do not have trust and confidence in the integrity of the process. Voter ID gives all voters a reason to trust that their vote will matter.
PROP. 39 INCLUDES AUDITS AND CITIZENSHIP VERIFICATION
Prop. 39 holds election officials accountable for keeping California’s voter lists accurate and updated. Election officials will also be required to check voter rolls to ensure only citizens are registered. Prop. 39 requires an independent audit be conducted every two years to give the public the confidence they deserve in the way our elections are conducted.
YES ON PROP. 39: FOR A NON-PARTISAN SOLUTION TO VOTER ID
Politicians and partisan organizations who oppose Prop. 39 are desperately trying to inject toxic partisanship into this debate. That’s because they benefit from unfounded election conspiracy theories and rapidly declining trust in our elections.
In contrast, supporters of Prop. 39 include solid majorities of Democratic, Republican and Independent voters and a diverse coalition including Latino American Political Association, California Women’s Leadership Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the Transparency Foundation, and trusted voting rights organizations. Vote YES on Prop. 39 to create a national model for implementing Voter ID in a bipartisan way.
Margit Whitlock , Democratic Coalition Chair
Californians for Voter ID
Tafa Jefferson , Republican Coalition Chair
Californians for Voter ID
Joe Green , Independent Coalition Chair
Californians for Voter ID
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 39
NO on PROP. 39—Stop Trump from rigging our elections. Don’t believe the lies. Prop. 39 MAKES VOTING HARDER, MORE EXPENSIVE, AND LESS SAFE for Californians.
PROP. 39 IS FUNDED BY MAGA RIGHTWING BILLIONAIRES. Follow the money. MAGA billionaires have spent millions spreading election lies. Republican operatives have pushed this voter suppression agenda for years. They want Trump to have unlimited power so they get more tax breaks for the rich while cutting funding to healthcare and schools for the rest of us.
California election officials already verify voters. Prop. 39 just ADDS EXTRA HURDLES for citizens. THE FACTS DON’T LIE. When Texas tried this, they threw out 12 times more mail ballots than California.
Prop. 39 creates new threats of identity theft. No citizen should have to choose between their privacy and their right to vote.
The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office found that Prop. 39 could COST HUNDREDS OF MILLIONS EACH YEAR—read it for yourself. MAGA extremists want to use your taxpayer dollars to buy Trump an expensive gift: blocking eligible voters and giving the Big Lie a win in California. We won’t fall for it.
PROP. 39 TRIES TO DISTRACT US from how Trump and his billionaire friends have failed Americans. Hospitals are closing. Fire victims are still waiting for help. Groceries and housing costs are more expensive than ever. Now they want to use Prop. 39 to control our elections and avoid accountability.
NO KINGS. NO LIES. NO PROP. 39.
Alex Padilla , U.S. Senator for California
Catherine Kennedy , President
California Nurses Association
Adam Weinberger , President
California School Employees Association
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 39
VOTE NO. Donald Trump lies about elections and uses those lies to grab power.
STOP TRUMP’S POWER GRAB. Trump wants revenge on California—he has delayed LA wildfire relief, undone laws to keep our air and water clean, and constantly attacked our immigrant friends and neighbors. Now he wants to undo our freedoms and democracy with Prop. 39. Trump’s cronies want to rig California elections so they can seize and keep control of Congress and the White House. Trump will do whatever it takes to tear apart our right to vote, dodge accountability, and hold onto authoritarian power.
CALIFORNIANS WON’T FALL FOR IT. We have a chance to fight back and stop Trump by voting NO on Prop. 39. Don’t let California become the next state where politicians pick which voters count.
WASTES HUNDREDS OF MILLIONS OF DOLLARS.
Trump and his accomplices want California to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to chase their election lies and conspiracy theories. Californians are struggling, and Trump wants YOU to pay for his conspiracies.
PUTS YOUR IDENTITY AT RISK. Prop. 39 will make every vote by mail voter include their personal details on their return envelope—making voters easy targets for identity theft. Voters would have to choose between voting and protecting their privacy.
BLOCKS CITIZENS FROM VOTING. Prop. 39 adds new hurdles—voters would have to include a personal ID number on their ballot envelope that has to exactly match state records. Get one digit wrong, and a valid ballot could get thrown out. If you don’t take extra steps to tell officials which ID you want to use for voting—you may not get a mail ballot at all. And if the address on your ID is not up to date or your name is misspelled—your vote might be rejected.
PUSHES OUT VOTERS. “Free” state IDs aren’t free: voters still pay for transportation, time off work, and costs like childcare or getting required documents. Seniors, students, low-income workers, voters of color, and the millions of women who changed their names at marriage are hit hardest. These unfair barriers help politicians choose their voters instead of the other way around.
TRUMP LIES TO GRAB POWER. DON’T LET THOSE LIES TAKE AWAY YOUR VOTE.
PROTECT YOUR VOICE. PROTECT YOUR VOTE. VOTE NO.
Learn more at CAforVotingRights.org
David Trujillo , Executive Director
ACLU California Action
Darius Kemp , California State Director
Common Cause
Lorrel Plimier , Co-President
League of Women Voters of California
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 39
PROP. 39 IS BIPARTISAN—NOT ABOUT DONALD TRUMP OR GAVIN NEWSOM
Prop. 39 gives California a bipartisan solution for election security. While politicians in D.C. fight over partisan control of elections, Californians can adopt our own solution: Voter ID. Opponents will claim this measure is about Donald Trump or Gavin Newsom. It isn’t. Prop. 39 is a California solution to growing mistrust in our elections. Democrats, Republicans, and Nonpartisans encourage you to reject the big-money partisan allegations and vote yes on Prop. 39 to encourage voter participation and protect our elections.
PROP. 39 IMPROVES ELECTION MANAGEMENT
Prop. 39 improves the accuracy of our voter lists and requires independent audits to strengthen election management.
VOTER ID INCREASES TRUST IN ELECTIONS
States with voter ID laws have not seen decreases in voter participation. When voters trust elections, participation increases.
YES ON PROP. 39
Opponents will claim this is about national politics or that Voter ID suppresses voters. Don’t be fooled. Prop. 39 is supported by Democrats, Republicans, and Nonpartisans, as well as men, women, young, and old—Californians across many communities.
If you believe California should strengthen trust in elections while keeping voting accessible for eligible voters, vote YES on Prop. 39 for a clean, bipartisan California solution.

Cynthia Kaui , Executive Director
California Women’s Leadership Association
Ed Cervantes , President

This initiative measure is submitted to the people in
accordance with the provisions of Section 8 of Article II
of the California Constitution.

To enforce existing voter qualifications, including US
citizenship, established by California’s Constitution,
the people hereby amend the California Constitution:

electoral process, which encourages civic participation

detect voter fraud by maintaining accurate voter

SEC. 2.1. Section 3.1 is added to Article II of the
California Constitution, to read:
SEC. 3.1. (a) The Secretary of State, and county
elections officials, shall each have the duty to maintain
accurate voter registration lists, shall use best efforts to
verify citizenship attestations using government data,
and shall annually report what percentage of each
county’s voter rolls have been citizenship-verified.
(b) Each time a voter casts a ballot in person in any
election in the State, the voter shall present
government-issued identification, or if voting by mail,
the voter shall provide the last four digits of a unique
identifying number from government-issued
identification that matches the one designated by the
voter for their voter registration. The type of
identification designated by each voter must be
indicated in their voter registration record, noted on the
mail ballot envelope provided to them, and available to
them on request by phone or electronically. Election
officials shall only count a regular or provisional ballot
after verifying the identity of the person voting pursuant
to the requirements of this section, and verifying that
the person has cast only one ballot in the election.
Government-issued identification means
documentation that allows conclusive verification of the
voter’s identity. Upon request by an eligible voter, the
State shall provide, at no charge, a voter ID card for use
in casting a ballot.
(c) This section shall be self-executing. The Legislature
shall also promptly enact laws to implement this
section, provide for voting by military and overseas
voters consistent with federal law, and ensure that all
State and local officials comply and support the
compliance with this section. Citizens may seek judicial
review and remedy of the State’s or any county’s
compliance with this section. During every odd-
numbered year, the California State Auditor shall audit
the State’s and each county’s compliance with this
section and report its findings and recommendations
for improving the integrity of elections to the public.
SEC. 3. Severability.
The provisions of this act are severable. If any portion,
section, subdivision, paragraph, clause, sentence,
phrase, word, or application of this act is for any reason
held to be invalid by a decision of any court of
competent jurisdiction, that decision shall not affect
the validity of the remaining portions of this act, which
shall be given effect without the invalid portion or
application.

This initiative measure is submitted to the people in

This initiative measure adds a section to the California
Constitution and amends and adds sections to the
Government Code and Revenue and Taxation Code;
therefore, new provisions proposed to be added are
printed in italic type to indicate that they are new.

The 2026 Billionaire Tax Act
The people of California do enact as follows:
SECTION 1. Title.
This act shall be known, and may be cited, as the 2026
Billionaire Tax Act.
SEC. 2. Findings.
(a) The people recognize that access to adequate
health care, quality public education, and nourishing
food is essential to human dignity and to the prosperity
and resilience of the entire state. The cascading
impacts of looming federal funding cuts for health care,
education, and food programs now threaten these
foundations and place the welfare of all Californians at
risk.
(b) California’s health care safety net is under
extraordinary threat, as Medi-Cal—the backbone of
coverage for nearly 15 million low-income Californians,
including more than half of the state’s children, 2.2
million seniors and people with disabilities, and one in
five of all working adults—faces billions in federal
funding cuts which will only exacerbate existing
challenges.
(c) Medi-Cal is projected to lose up to $19 billion in
annual federal funding due to the implementation of
the most recent federal budget legislation and
administrative action, shifting costs to the state
General Fund and local governments or forcing
reductions in needed services. Over the next ten years,
federal cuts to Medi-Cal alone are projected to total
approximately $190 billion.

stresses California’s already underfunded health care
safety net. The 2025–26 state budget included several
new restrictions, including cuts to providers and
significant reductions in benefits and services for Medi-
Cal enrollees. State cuts to Medi-Cal are estimated to

year from 2028–29 onward.

maintain current levels of service because Medi-Cal

OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Prohibits voting by mail unless voter designates a government-issued identification number for their voter registration.
Invalidates mail ballots if envelope does not include last four digits of a government-issued identification number matching the number designated in the voter’s registration (e.g., if voter designates Social Security number for registration, but provides driver’s license number on envelope, their ballot would not count).
Prohibits voting in person without presenting government-issued identification.
Requires elections officials to annually report percentage of each county’s voters whose citizenship status they have verified.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
State and local government costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. Costs depend on future decisions by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
Now I have the full text. Key details:

1. It's a constitutional amendment (Article II, Section 3.1).
2. Requires government-issued ID for in-person voting.
3. Requires mail voters to write last 4 digits of a designated government-issued ID number on the envelope; the ballot is INVALIDATED if it doesn't match the designated ID type. Notably: if a voter designates SSN for registration but writes DL number, ballot doesn't count.
4. Requires citizenship verification "best efforts" using government data, with annual reporting.
5. Creates a free state voter ID card.
6. Requires State Auditor audits in odd-numbered years.
7. Self-executing, with private right of action for citizens to seek judicial review.
8. Requires Legislature to enact implementing laws.
9. Severability clause.

Important issues to research:
- Does it have a cure process for mail ballots with wrong/missing ID numbers? The text says "Election officials shall only count a regular or provisional ballot after verifying the identity..." — it does not appear to provide a cure mechanism. Under current California law (Elections Code 3019), there's a signature mismatch cure process (compare-and-cure). Note the "PRO" argument claims the measure would reduce signature-mismatch rejections. But the text doesn't explicitly eliminate signature verification, nor does it add a cure process for the ID number mismatch. Actually, it says officials shall only count a ballot after verifying identity pursuant to the section. This could effectively be a strict requirement with no cure, which could disqualify many ballots.

- Impact on vote-by-mail: California is a vote-by-mail state (Voter's Choice Act / all-mail elections). About 13 million of 16 million voters voted by mail in Nov 2024. So this is a huge change.

- Privacy: writing last 4 digits of SSN on the ballot return envelope. Envelopes are handled by many people; also envelopes are subject to public records disclosure? Under California law, ballot envelopes are retained and... Let me check whether they are public records. Actually, in California, "voter registration records" have confidentiality provisions but signature verification envelopes — hmm. There is a claim that they'd be exposed to identity theft. Let me research whether ballot envelopes are subject to public records requests in California.

- Federal law conflict: Help America Vote Act (HAVA) §301(b) requires first-time mail registrants to provide ID; the National Voter Registration Act; and importantly, states cannot require more than HAVA's requirements? Actually HAVA sets a floor for first-time voters who registered by mail. States can impose stricter ID requirements generally. But there could be a preemption question. Also, the SAVE Act (federal) — proof of citizenship. Not preemptive.

- Note that under current CA law, only about 1-2% of voters are asked for ID at the polls (first-time mail registrants who didn't provide ID). 

- Litigation: Are there lawsuits challenging Prop 39's placement on the ballot? Let me research. There may be a challenge to the title/summary or to the single-subject rule. Also possibly a pre-election challenge regarding the "self-executing" nature and the fact that the Legislature hasn't defined what IDs qualify — meaning it's inoperative/impractical?

- Polling: Voter ID is generally very popular (70-80% support nationally). In California, polling might show support. Let me look for polls on Prop 39 specifically.

- Funding: Support $36.5M, Opposition $33.5M. Who funds? "The Transparency Foundation" — Johnathan Hale. Let me research funding sources. Opposition claims "MAGA billionaires." Let me verify.

- Endorsements: Newspapers? Let's check.

Let me do a bunch of searches.

Let me also consider: the question asks "What should I vote on this prop?" and "You can only answer yes or no." So I must give a definitive yes or no, with reasoning. I should be thorough and balanced, then commit.

Let me research more.
I now have the full text. Let me research the campaign funding, litigation, polling, and expert/news analysis.

Now I have the full text. Key details:

1. It's a constitutional amendment (Article II, Section 3.1).
2. Requires government-issued ID for in-person voting.
3. Requires mail voters to write last 4 digits of a designated government-issued ID number on the envelope; the ballot is INVALIDATED if it doesn't match the designated ID type. Notably: if a voter designates SSN for registration but writes DL number, ballot doesn't count.
4. Requires citizenship verification "best efforts" using government data, with annual reporting.
5. Creates a free state voter ID card.
6. Requires State Auditor audits in odd-numbered years.
7. Self-executing, with private right of action for citizens to seek judicial review.
8. Requires Legislature to enact implementing laws.
9. Severability clause.

Important issues to research:
- Does it have a cure process for mail ballots with wrong/missing ID numbers? The text says "Election officials shall only count a regular or provisional ballot after verifying the identity..." — it does not appear to provide a cure mechanism. Under current California law (Elections Code 3019), there's a signature mismatch cure process (compare-and-cure). Note the "PRO" argument claims the measure would reduce signature-mismatch rejections. But the text doesn't explicitly eliminate signature verification, nor does it add a cure process for the ID number mismatch. Actually, it says officials shall only count a ballot after verifying identity pursuant to the section. This could effectively be a strict requirement with no cure, which could disqualify many ballots.

- Impact on vote-by-mail: California is a vote-by-mail state (Voter's Choice Act / all-mail elections). About 13 million of 16 million voters voted by mail in Nov 2024. So this is a huge change.

- Privacy: writing last 4 digits of SSN on the ballot return envelope. Envelopes are handled by many people; also envelopes are subject to public records disclosure? Under California law, ballot envelopes are retained and... Let me check whether they are public records. Actually, in California, "voter registration records" have confidentiality provisions but signature verification envelopes — hmm. There is a claim that they'd be exposed to identity theft. Let me research whether ballot envelopes are subject to public records requests in California.

- Federal law conflict: Help America Vote Act (HAVA) §301(b) requires first-time mail registrants to provide ID; the National Voter Registration Act; and importantly, states cannot require more than HAVA's requirements? Actually HAVA sets a floor for first-time voters who registered by mail. States can impose stricter ID requirements generally. But there could be a preemption question. Also, the SAVE Act (federal) — proof of citizenship. Not preemptive.

- Note that under current CA law, only about 1-2% of voters are asked for ID at the polls (first-time mail registrants who didn't provide ID). 

- Litigation: Are there lawsuits challenging Prop 39's placement on the ballot? Let me research. There may be a challenge to the title/summary or to the single-subject rule. Registered Voter List Administration Initiative
Summary
Proposition 39 began as a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment filed with the California Attorney General's (https://oag.ca.gov/) office on July 16, 2025. The initiative received a revised ballot title and was approved for signature gathering on September 19, 2025. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 874,641 valid signatures.The campaign submitted nearly 1.37 million signatures on March 2, 2026 and the initiative officially qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 39 on April 24, 2026.
On July 27, 2026, Californians for Voter ID (https://www.voteridca.org/) filed a lawsuit against the Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/) challenging the new ballot title for Proposition 39, which was drafted by Attorney General Rob Bonta after his office received the amendment. The plaintiffs argued that the new title of “prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification,” was false and misleading, as it did not include the original title’s reference to additional voter identification and citizenship verification requirements. The Attorney General’s Office maintained that the revised language more accurately describes the measure’s provisions. On August 6, 2026, Sacramento County Superior Court found for the state and ruled that the ballot title is sufficient, thus the measure will remain on the ballot unchanged.
Proposition 39 would establish new identification and citizenship-verification requirements for California elections. State and local election officials would be required to make “best efforts,” using government records, to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually on the percentage verified in each county. Voters would also have to select a government-issued form of identification when registering in order to vote by mail, and the state would provide a free voter identification card to anyone who requests one.
The measure would also require voters to provide identifying information each time they cast a ballot. In-person voters would need to present government-issued identification, while mail voters would provide the last four digits of their selected identification number on the ballot envelope for verification. Elections officials would confirm that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information. The State Auditor would review state and county compliance every odd numbered year. Proposition 39 mandates that the Legislature would need to clarify details not included in the proposition and they would have to pass additional laws before the measure could be fully implemented.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs by an estimated tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars annually, although the exact amount would depend on how the measure is implemented. These costs amount to less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Major costs would be influenced by decisions about the new voter identification card, administrative requirements, and the number of voters requesting cards. As ineligible voters or eligible voters lack the required identification are removed from voting, some savings could result.
What your vote means
YES: A "yes" vote supports amending the state constitution to require government-issued ID for in-person voting or the last four digits of a designated government ID for mail-in voting, mandate annual citizenship-verification reporting for county voter rolls, and require odd-year compliance audits by the State Auditor.
NO: A "no" vote opposes these changes, maintaining current law where government ID is not required to vote, and voters attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury without requiring election officials to verify attestations against government data or report verification rates.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters of Proposition 39 argue that requiring voter identification would strengthen confidence in California elections by adding safeguards they believe are currently lacking. They point to voter ID requirements in other states and countries as evidence that such rules are a common feature of democratic election systems rather than an unusual restriction. Supporters also contend that changes such as universal mail ballots and ballot collection have increased the need for additional identity checks. While they do not necessarily claim that widespread voter fraud is occurring, they maintain that Proposition 39 would make the election process more secure, transparent, and less vulnerable to public doubt.
Opponents of Proposition 39 argue that the measure would impose unnecessary barriers on eligible voters without addressing a demonstrated problem in California elections. They contend that existing procedures already provide multiple safeguards for verifying voters and that additional identification and citizenship checks could lead to eligible ballots being rejected, with disproportionate effects on people with disabilities and others who may have difficulty meeting the new requirements.
Critics also raise privacy concerns about placing partial identification numbers on mail ballot envelopes and argue that implementing the measure would create significant new administrative costs. Finally, opponents characterize Proposition 39 as part of a national push for stricter voting rules that they believe would make voting more difficult rather than meaningfully improve election security.

Even if you think voter fraud is a problem in California (it’s not), Prop 39 would turn our elections into a never-ending lawsuit
Proposition 39 would require Californians to present or incorporate some form of identification when voting. It is almost certain to disenfranchise eligible voters. The Chronicle’s editorial board recommends a no vote.
Todd Trumbull/S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 12, 2026
Is voter fraud rampant in California?
A May poll by the Public Policy Institute of California (https://data.ddhq.io/polls/2026/05/30/Public-Policy-Institute-of-California-California) found that 41% of likely voters here were either “very” or “somewhat” concerned that it’s too easy for ineligible voters to cast ballots.
That’s not an insignificant number.

So, how can California shore up trust?
Carl DeMaio, the firebrand Republican Assembly member from San Diego, claims to have the answer: Proposition 39 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
The measure would create a host of new voter-identification requirements in California and mandate regular election audits. Prop 39 was placed on the November ballot via a signature-gathering effort by volunteers from DeMaio’s advocacy organization (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/02/carl-demaio-california-maga-voter-id-prop-39-01103730?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e), Reform California, and paid operatives funded by Julie Luckey (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2025/11/24/the-donor-powering-a-voter-id-push-in-california-00667090), whose son Palmer was recently named as a leader of the Trump administration’s new Project Meridian war council (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/pentagon-weapon-military-war-22464710.php).
Even though wealthy out-of-state Republicans have largely funded the yes campaign, DeMaio inexplicably insisted to the editorial board that the measure is “a balanced, bipartisan approach.”

Prop 39 is “the best way to shut down the conspiracy theories that irresponsible politicians spread,” DeMaio said.
Well, no.
The best way is for those irresponsible politicians, paramount among them DeMaio’s ally, President Donald Trump, to stop sowing unfounded disbelief.
Because by every available measure, California’s voting system is working.
The California State Library’s research bureau examined reports from 14 counties (https://www.library.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/crb-reports/CRB-Voter-Fraud-Presentation-Senate-Elections-2026-04-03.pdf) where grand juries investigated voter fraud risks from 2020 to 2024 and found an overwhelming consensus: no evidence of systemic or significant fraud. Even the right-wing Heritage Foundation — the organization behind Project 2025 — identified just 71 instances of known voter fraud in California (https://electionfraud.heritage.org/search?case_type=All&fraud_type=All&state=CA) from 1982 to 2025.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
All of those cases were prosecuted — evidence that California takes election integrity seriously. In fact, the state rejected its highest percentage of mail ballots in more than a decade (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-mail-ballot-rejections-22359196.php) for the June 2 primary — largely because they were postmarked after Election Day or arrived too late. There was also an uptick in signatures that election officials couldn’t verify.
Yet Prop 39 supporters insist on the need for additional identity verification.
To understand Prop 39’s proposed changes and the impact, let’s first look at the state’s existing processes:
Under California law (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration), anyone registering to vote must prove their identity via their driver’s license, state identification number or the last four digits of their Social Security number. Election officials check this identification against state and federal databases. Voters must also attest under penalty of perjury — which carries a potential prison sentence — that they’re a U.S. citizen living in California who’s at least 18 years old and not currently in prison or found incapable of voting by a court.
Every registered voter in California then receives a mail-in ballot, which most residents prefer (more than 80% voted this way in the past election). Before counting it, election officials check whether the voter’s signature on the outside of the ballot matches the signature on file (usually from a driver’s license). If it doesn’t, election officials give voters a chance to “cure” it by notifying them of the issue and providing a correction form (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2026-general/november-3-2026-general-combo-statement.pdf), which they have 22 days to return.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
People voting in person typically don’t have to present ID, but they do have to sign a registration list at the polls.
Prop 39 would change all that. To vote by mail, Californians would have to preselect a form of government-issued identification and write the last four digits of that ID on the outside of their ballot.
To vote in person, Californians would need to show a government-issued ID. Prop 39 mandates the state provide free “voter identification cards” — which do not currently exist — to those who request them. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop39-110326.pdf) estimated that creating these cards, in addition to other expenses resulting from Prop 39, could cost local and state governments hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
The measure also requires state and local elections officials to employ “best efforts” to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens and to publish annual reports revealing the percentage of verified voters. It mandates the state auditor to review compliance every other year.
What forms of government-issued ID would be acceptable under Prop 39, and how would voters preselect the ID they want to use for their 4-digit PIN? Do they get a chance to cure their ballots if they write the wrong digits on their vote-by-mail envelope? And what would be considered “best efforts” to verify someone’s citizenship status — given that even the federal government doesn’t have a comprehensive list of citizens?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 39 directs the state Legislature to “promptly” enact laws to answer these questions. It also creates a private right of action that permits any person who believes state or local government isn’t complying with the measure to take those entities to court.
Justin Levitt, a constitutional and election law expert at the Loyola Law School, called this a “generic litigation trap” that opens the door to countless frivolous lawsuits.
Just as the California Environmental Quality Act enables aggrieved NIMBYs to weaponize the legal system against development projects they dislike, Prop 39 will do the same with elections.
“You will have plenty of advocacy organizations that are eager to sue over perceived noncompliance with this initiative early and often,” Levitt told the editorial board.
And Prop 39 is almost certain to disenfranchise eligible voters.
Large numbers of California U.S. citizens lack either IDs or proof of citizenship. A 2026 University of Maryland analysis (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/Who%20Lacks%20ID%20and%20Proof%20of%20Citizenship%20in%20California%20Today_.pdf) found that about 2.7 million Californians, or about 11% of eligible voters, don’t have a driver’s license, while 13% have one that’s expired or has an outdated address or name. People of color, young residents, disabled Californians and lower-income residents are disproportionately represented in these groups.
The study also found 24% of Californians don’t have a passport and that more than 3 million voting-age Californians would have difficulty readily accessing documents proving their citizenship.
In short, Prop 39 would do little to stop the minimal fraud that exists while creating millions “more chances for valid ballots to be rejected,” Abdi Soltani, executive director of ACLU of Northern California, told the editorial board.
After Texas passed a similar voter-ID law in 2021, its rate of rejected ballots skyrocketed from less than 1% to more than 12% (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/), effectively invalidating 1 in 8 votes cast in the 2022 primary. A peer-reviewed study (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/737439) found it also reduced voter turnout in subsequent elections.

Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Voter Identification
Registered Voter List Administration Initiative
Summary
Proposition 39 began as a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment filed with the California Attorney General's (https://oag.ca.gov/) office on July 16, 2025. The initiative received a revised ballot title and was approved for signature gathering on September 19, 2025. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 874,641 valid signatures.The campaign submitted nearly 1.37 million signatures on March 2, 2026 and the initiative officially qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 39 on April 24, 2026.
On July 27, 2026, Californians for Voter ID (https://www.voteridca.org/) filed a lawsuit against the Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/) challenging the new ballot title for Proposition 39, which was drafted by Attorney General Rob Bonta after his office received the amendment. The plaintiffs argued that the new title of “prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification,” was false and misleading, as it did not include the original title’s reference to additional voter identification and citizenship verification requirements. The Attorney General’s Office maintained that the revised language more accurately describes the measure’s provisions. On August 6, 2026, Sacramento County Superior Court found for the state and ruled that the ballot title is sufficient, thus the measure will remain on the ballot unchanged.
Proposition 39 would establish new identification and citizenship-verification requirements for California elections. State and local election officials would be required to make “best efforts,” using government records, to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually on the percentage verified in each county. Voters would also have to select a government-issued form of identification when registering in order to vote by mail, and the state would provide a free voter identification card to anyone who requests one.
The measure would also require voters to provide identifying information each time they cast a ballot. In-person voters would need to present government-issued identification, while mail voters would provide the last four digits of their selected identification number on the ballot envelope for verification. Elections officials would confirm that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information. The State Auditor would review state and county compliance every odd numbered year. Proposition 39 mandates that the Legislature would need to clarify details not included in the proposition and they would have to pass additional laws before the measure could be fully implemented.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs by an estimated tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars annually, although the exact amount would depend on how the measure is implemented. These costs amount to less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Major costs would be influenced by decisions about the new voter identification card, administrative requirements, and the number of voters requesting cards. As ineligible voters or eligible voters lack the required identification are removed from voting, some savings could result.
What your vote means
YES: A "yes" vote supports amending the state constitution to require government-issued ID for in-person voting or the last four digits of a designated government ID for mail-in voting, mandate annual citizenship-verification reporting for county voter rolls, and require odd-year compliance audits by the State Auditor.
NO: A "no" vote opposes these changes, maintaining current law where government ID is not required to vote, and voters attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury without requiring election officials to verify attestations against government data or report verification rates.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters of Proposition 39 argue that requiring voter identification would strengthen confidence in California elections by adding safeguards they believe are currently lacking. They point to voter ID requirements in other states and countries as evidence that such rules are a common feature of democratic election systems rather than an unusual restriction. Supporters also contend that changes such as universal mail ballots and ballot collection have increased the need for additional identity checks. While they do not necessarily claim that widespread voter fraud is occurring, they maintain that Proposition 39 would make the election process more secure, transparent, and less vulnerable to public doubt.
Opponents of Proposition 39 argue that the measure would impose unnecessary barriers on eligible voters without addressing a demonstrated problem in California elections. They contend that existing procedures already provide multiple safeguards for verifying voters and that additional identification and citizenship checks could lead to eligible ballots being rejected, with disproportionate effects on people with disabilities and others who may have difficulty meeting the new requirements.
Critics also raise privacy concerns about placing partial identification numbers on mail ballot envelopes and argue that implementing the measure would create significant new administrative costs. Finally, opponents characterize Proposition 39 as part of a national push for stricter voting rules that they believe would make voting more difficult rather than meaningfully improve election security.

Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Voter Identification
Registered Voter List Administration Initiative
Summary
Proposition 39 began as a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment filed with the California Attorney General's (https://oag.ca.gov/) office on July 16, 2025. The initiative received a revised ballot title and was approved for signature gathering on September 19, 2025. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 874,641 valid signatures.The campaign submitted nearly 1.37 million signatures on March 2, 2026 and the initiative officially qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 39 on April 24, 2026.
On July 27, 2026, Californians for Voter ID (https://www.voteridca.org/) filed a lawsuit against the Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/) challenging the new ballot title for Proposition 39, which was drafted by Attorney General Rob Bonta after his office received the amendment. The plaintiffs argued that the new title of “prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification,” was false and misleading, as it did not include the original title’s reference to additional voter identification and citizenship verification requirements. The Attorney General’s Office maintained that the revised language more accurately describes the measure’s provisions. On August 6, 2026, Sacramento County Superior Court found for the state and ruled that the ballot title is sufficient, thus the measure will remain on the ballot unchanged.
Proposition 39 would establish new identification and citizenship-verification requirements for California elections. State and local election officials would be required to make “best efforts,” using government records, to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually on the percentage verified in each county. Voters would also have to select a government-issued form of identification when registering in order to vote by mail, and the state would provide a free voter identification card to anyone who requests one.
The measure would also require voters to provide identifying information each time they cast a ballot. In-person voters would need to present government-issued identification, while mail voters would provide the last four digits of their selected identification number on the ballot envelope for verification. Elections officials would confirm that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information. The State Auditor would review state and county compliance every odd numbered year. Proposition 39 mandates that the Legislature would need to clarify details not included in the proposition and they would have to pass additional laws before the measure could be fully implemented.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs by an estimated tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars annually, although the exact amount would depend on how the measure is implemented. These costs amount to less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Major costs would be influenced by decisions about the new voter identification card, administrative requirements, and the number of voters requesting cards. As ineligible voters or eligible voters lack the required identification are removed from voting, some savings could result.
What your vote means
YES: A "yes" vote supports amending the state constitution to require government-issued ID for in-person voting or the last four digits of a designated government ID for mail-in voting, mandate annual citizenship-verification reporting for county voter rolls, and require odd-year compliance audits by the State Auditor.
NO: A "no" vote opposes these changes, maintaining current law where government ID is not required to vote, and voters attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury without requiring election officials to verify attestations against government data or report verification rates.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters of Proposition 39 argue that requiring voter identification would strengthen confidence in California elections by adding safeguards they believe are currently lacking. They point to voter ID requirements in other states and countries as evidence that such rules are a common feature of democratic election systems rather than an unusual restriction. Supporters also contend that changes such as universal mail ballots and ballot collection have increased the need for additional identity checks. While they do not necessarily claim that widespread voter fraud is occurring, they maintain that Proposition 39 would make the election process more secure, transparent, and less vulnerable to public doubt.
Opponents of Proposition 39 argue that the measure would impose unnecessary barriers on eligible voters without addressing a demonstrated problem in California elections. They contend that existing procedures already provide multiple safeguards for verifying voters and that additional identification and citizenship checks could lead to eligible ballots being rejected, with disproportionate effects on people with disabilities and others who may have difficulty meeting the new requirements.
Critics also raise privacy concerns about placing partial identification numbers on mail ballot envelopes and argue that implementing the measure would create significant new administrative costs. Finally, opponents characterize Proposition 39 as part of a national push for stricter voting rules that they believe would make voting more difficult rather than meaningfully improve election security.

Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Voter Identification
Registered Voter List Administration Initiative
Summary
Proposition 39 began as a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment filed with the California Attorney General's (https://oag.ca.gov/) office on July 16, 2025. The initiative received a revised ballot title and was approved for signature gathering on September 19, 2025. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 874,641 valid signatures.The campaign submitted nearly 1.37 million signatures on March 2, 2026 and the initiative officially qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 39 on April 24, 2026.
On July 27, 2026, Californians for Voter ID (https://www.voteridca.org/) filed a lawsuit against the Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/) challenging the new ballot title for Proposition 39, which was drafted by Attorney General Rob Bonta after his office received the amendment. The plaintiffs argued that the new title of “prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification,” was false and misleading, as it did not include the original title’s reference to additional voter identification and citizenship verification requirements. The Attorney General’s Office maintained that the revised language more accurately describes the measure’s provisions. On August 6, 2026, Sacramento County Superior Court found for the state and ruled that the ballot title is sufficient, thus the measure will remain on the ballot unchanged.
Proposition 39 would establish new identification and citizenship-verification requirements for California elections. State and local election officials would be required to make “best efforts,” using government records, to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually on the percentage verified in each county. Voters would also have to select a government-issued form of identification when registering in order to vote by mail, and the state would provide a free voter identification card to anyone who requests one.
The measure would also require voters to provide identifying information each time they cast a ballot. In-person voters would need to present government-issued identification, while mail voters would provide the last four digits of their selected identification number on the ballot envelope for verification. Elections officials would confirm that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information. The State Auditor would review state and county compliance every odd numbered year. Proposition 39 mandates that the Legislature would need to clarify details not included in the proposition and they would have to pass additional laws before the measure could be fully implemented.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs by an estimated tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars annually, although the exact amount would depend on how the measure is implemented. These costs amount to less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Major costs would be influenced by decisions about the new voter identification card, administrative requirements, and the number of voters requesting cards. As ineligible voters or eligible voters lack the required identification are removed from voting, some savings could result.
What your vote means
YES: A "yes" vote supports amending the state constitution to require government-issued ID for in-person voting or the last four digits of a designated government ID for mail-in voting, mandate annual citizenship-verification reporting for county voter rolls, and require odd-year compliance audits by the State Auditor.
NO: A "no" vote opposes these changes, maintaining current law where government ID is not required to vote, and voters attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury without requiring election officials to verify attestations against government data or report verification rates.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters of Proposition 39 argue that requiring voter identification would strengthen confidence in California elections by adding safeguards they believe are currently lacking. They point to voter ID requirements in other states and countries as evidence that such rules are a common feature of democratic election systems rather than an unusual restriction. Supporters also contend that changes such as universal mail ballots and ballot collection have increased the need for additional identity checks. While they do not necessarily claim that widespread voter fraud is occurring, they maintain that Proposition 39 would make the election process more secure, transparent, and less vulnerable to public doubt.
Opponents of Proposition 39 argue that the measure would impose unnecessary barriers on eligible voters without addressing a demonstrated problem in California elections. They contend that existing procedures already provide multiple safeguards for verifying voters and that additional identification and citizenship checks could lead to eligible ballots being rejected, with disproportionate effects on people with disabilities and others who may have difficulty meeting the new requirements.
Critics also raise privacy concerns about placing partial identification numbers on mail ballot envelopes and argue that implementing the measure would create significant new administrative costs. Finally, opponents characterize Proposition 39 as part of a national push for stricter voting rules that they believe would make voting more difficult rather than meaningfully improve election security.

Endorsement: Prop 39 would create CEQA for voting rights. No thanks
Even if you think voter fraud is a problem in California (it’s not), Prop 39 would turn our elections into a never-ending lawsuit
Proposition 39 would require Californians to present or incorporate some form of identification when voting. It is almost certain to disenfranchise eligible voters. The Chronicle’s editorial board recommends a no vote.
Todd Trumbull/S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 12, 2026
Is voter fraud rampant in California?
A May poll by the Public Policy Institute of California (https://data.ddhq.io/polls/2026/05/30/Public-Policy-Institute-of-California-California) found that 41% of likely voters here were either “very” or “somewhat” concerned that it’s too easy for ineligible voters to cast ballots.
That’s not an insignificant number.
Chronicle endorsements: Editorial Board’s recommendations for 2026 election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
So, how can California shore up trust?
Carl DeMaio, the firebrand Republican Assembly member from San Diego, claims to have the answer: Proposition 39 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
The measure would create a host of new voter-identification requirements in California and mandate regular election audits. Prop 39 was placed on the November ballot via a signature-gathering effort by volunteers from DeMaio’s advocacy organization (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/02/carl-demaio-california-maga-voter-id-prop-39-01103730?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e), Reform California, and paid operatives funded by Julie Luckey (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2025/11/24/the-donor-powering-a-voter-id-push-in-california-00667090), whose son Palmer was recently named as a leader of the Trump administration’s new Project Meridian war council (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/pentagon-weapon-military-war-22464710.php).
Even though wealthy out-of-state Republicans have largely funded the yes campaign, DeMaio inexplicably insisted to the editorial board that the measure is “a balanced, bipartisan approach.”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 39 is “the best way to shut down the conspiracy theories that irresponsible politicians spread,” DeMaio said.
Well, no.
The best way is for those irresponsible politicians, paramount among them DeMaio’s ally, President Donald Trump, to stop sowing unfounded disbelief.
Because by every available measure, California’s voting system is working.
The California State Library’s research bureau examined reports from 14 counties (https://www.library.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/crb-reports/CRB-Voter-Fraud-Presentation-Senate-Elections-2026-04-03.pdf) where grand juries investigated voter fraud risks from 2020 to 2024 and found an overwhelming consensus: no evidence of systemic or significant fraud. Even the right-wing Heritage Foundation — the organization behind Project 2025 — identified just 71 instances of known voter fraud in California (https://electionfraud.heritage.org/search?case_type=All&fraud_type=All&state=CA) from 1982 to 2025.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
All of those cases were prosecuted — evidence that California takes election integrity seriously. In fact, the state rejected its highest percentage of mail ballots in more than a decade (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-mail-ballot-rejections-22359196.php) for the June 2 primary — largely because they were postmarked after Election Day or arrived too late. There was also an uptick in signatures that election officials couldn’t verify.
Yet Prop 39 supporters insist on the need for additional identity verification.
To understand Prop 39’s proposed changes and the impact, let’s first look at the state’s existing processes:
Under California law (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration), anyone registering to vote must prove their identity via their driver’s license, state identification number or the last four digits of their Social Security number. Election officials check this identification against state and federal databases. Voters must also attest under penalty of perjury — which carries a potential prison sentence — that they’re a U.S. citizen living in California who’s at least 18 years old and not currently in prison or found incapable of voting by a court.
Every registered voter in California then receives a mail-in ballot, which most residents prefer (more than 80% voted this way in the past election). Before counting it, election officials check whether the voter’s signature on the outside of the ballot matches the signature on file (usually from a driver’s license). If it doesn’t, election officials give voters a chance to “cure” it by notifying them of the issue and providing a correction form (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2026-general/november-3-2026-general-combo-statement.pdf), which they have 22 days to return.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
People voting in person typically don’t have to present ID, but they do have to sign a registration list at the polls.
Prop 39 would change all that. To vote by mail, Californians would have to preselect a form of government-issued identification and write the last four digits of that ID on the outside of their ballot.
To vote in person, Californians would need to show a government-issued ID. Prop 39 mandates the state provide free “voter identification cards” — which do not currently exist — to those who request them. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop39-110326.pdf) estimated that creating these cards, in addition to other expenses resulting from Prop 39, could cost local and state governments hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
The measure also requires state and local elections officials to employ “best efforts” to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens and to publish annual reports revealing the percentage of verified voters. It mandates the state auditor to review compliance every other year.
What forms of government-issued ID would be acceptable under Prop 39, and how would voters preselect the ID they want to use for their 4-digit PIN? Do they get a chance to cure their ballots if they write the wrong digits on their vote-by-mail envelope? And what would be considered “best efforts” to verify someone’s citizenship status — given that even the federal government doesn’t have a comprehensive list of citizens?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 39 directs the state Legislature to “promptly” enact laws to answer these questions. It also creates a private right of action that permits any person who believes state or local government isn’t complying with the measure to take those entities to court.
Justin Levitt, a constitutional and election law expert at the Loyola Law School, called this a “generic litigation trap” that opens the door to countless frivolous lawsuits.
Just as the California Environmental Quality Act enables aggrieved NIMBYs to weaponize the legal system against development projects they dislike, Prop 39 will do the same with elections.
“You will have plenty of advocacy organizations that are eager to sue over perceived noncompliance with this initiative early and often,” Levitt told the editorial board.
And Prop 39 is almost certain to disenfranchise eligible voters.
Large numbers of California U.S. citizens lack either IDs or proof of citizenship. A 2026 University of Maryland analysis (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/Who%20Lacks%20ID%20and%20Proof%20of%20Citizenship%20in%20California%20Today_.pdf) found that about 2.7 million Californians, or about 11% of eligible voters, don’t have a driver’s license, while 13% have one that’s expired or has an outdated address or name. People of color, young residents, disabled Californians and lower-income residents are disproportionately represented in these groups.
The study also found 24% of Californians don’t have a passport and that more than 3 million voting-age Californians would have difficulty readily accessing documents proving their citizenship.
In short, Prop 39 would do little to stop the minimal fraud that exists while creating millions “more chances for valid ballots to be rejected,” Abdi Soltani, executive director of ACLU of Northern California, told the editorial board.
After Texas passed a similar voter-ID law in 2021, its rate of rejected ballots skyrocketed from less than 1% to more than 12% (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/), effectively invalidating 1 in 8 votes cast in the 2022 primary. A peer-reviewed study (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/737439) found it also reduced voter turnout in subsequent elections.
About Opinion
The editorial positions of The Chronicle, including election recommendations, represent the consensus of the editorial board , consisting of the publisher, the editorial page editor and staff members of the opinion pages. Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
California could do more to assuage concerns about election integrity. Counties have been begging the state for permission to join a nonprofit, multistate organization that helps officials improve the accuracy of their voter rolls (https://apcp.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2024-04/ab-2050-pellerin-apcp-analysis_1.pdf).
But Prop 39 is a nakedly bad-faith effort designed to encourage frivolous lawsuits, deepen distrust, increase political polarization and waste taxpayer dollars. Vote no.
Reach the Chronicle editorial board with a letter to the editor: www.sfchronicle.com/submit-your-opinion (https://www.sfchronicle.com/submit-your-opinion) .

Excellent, very substantive. Now let me check a few more things:

1. The CalMatters voter guide for a nonpartisan summary.
2. The California Budget & Policy Center issue brief on how many voters would be affected.
3. The strongest case FOR: the "pro" side arguments and the Daily News editorial endorsement, plus any Republican/conservative analysis. Also whether there's a legitimate concern: declining trust in elections, 41% concerned.
4. Whether the measure has a cure process — important. Let me confirm from the LAO report and text. The text has no explicit cure provision. That's a serious drafting flaw.
5. Federal law issues: e.g., would this conflict with UOCAVA/military overseas voting? The text says the Legislature shall "provide for voting by military and overseas voters consistent with federal law" — so that's addressed.
6. Whether the citizenship verification requirement would be problematic — there's no comprehensive federal database of citizens. The "best efforts" is vague.

Let me also check the LAO PDF for more detail and the CalMatters guide.

Let me also consider: is there a legitimate "yes" argument? Voter ID is popular; other democracies require ID. But this specific measure is unusually strict and poorly drafted for a mail-ballot state. Key concerns:
- No cure process specified for mail ballots (unlike current signature cure).
- Requires voters to pre-designate an ID type in their registration record; existing voters who haven't done this "may not get a mail ballot at all" per the opposition argument. Actually let's check: the text says "The type of identification designated by each voter must be indicated in their voter registration record, noted on the mail ballot envelope provided to them, and available to them on request by phone or electronically." And AG title says "Prohibits voting by mail unless voter designates a government-issued identification number for their voter registration." So ~22 million existing registered voters would need to take an affirmative new step to designate an ID type before they can receive/count a mail ballot. That's a massive one-time administrative burden on the entire electorate in a state where 80%+ vote by mail. The LAO doesn't quantify but it's a big deal.
- Privacy: last 4 digits of SSN on the outside of an envelope that passes through the mail and many hands; ballot envelopes become part of election records potentially subject to public records requests. Let me verify whether CA ballot envelopes are public records. Under Elections Code § 3025 / Gov Code, "signature verification envelopes" — hmm. Actually, California law: Elections Code § 2166 et seq. deals with voter registration confidentiality. Ballot envelopes are retained by county elections officials for 22 months and are... I recall that some states treat them as public records. Let me search to verify this claim.

Actually, let me be careful not to overstate. Let me search for whether California ballot return envelopes are subject to the Public Records Act.

7. Also worth checking: does the measure conflict with the state constitution's free elections clause, and has anyone predicted litigation? The Chronicle's Levitt "generic litigation trap" quote covers that.

8. Let me also check the CalMatters guide and the Budget Center brief for numbers on who lacks ID.

Let me do a few searches in parallel.
Let me examine the nonpartisan analyses and the strongest case in favor.

Proposition 39
Require identification for voting
This initiative would require voters to show government-issued identification at the polls and order election officials to verify that all registered voters are U.S. citizens. Voters who cast a mail-in ballot would need to give the last four digits of a government ID, such as a driver’s license number. California currently requires residents to provide an identification card and Social Security number to register to vote, but does not request it at polling places. It was placed on the ballot by conservative groups.
