Endorsement: Elect Michael Melillo to San Jose Unified School District Board of Education (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-michael-melillo-to-san-jose-unified-school-district-board-of-education/)
Endorsement: Reject San Mateo Community College District’s $848 million Measure V (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-reject-san-mateo-community-college-districts-848-million-measure-v/)
Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
This initiative is an expensive solution to a phantom problem. Reject Prop. 39.
Manufactured crisis
Multiple groups have studied the issue and found scant evidence of widespread fraud. The California State Library (https://www.library.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/crb-reports/CRB-Voter-Fraud-Presentation-Senate-Elections-2026-04-03.pdf) looked at 14 counties where grand juries issued reports on the risk of voter fraud in the 2020, 2022 and 2024 elections and found secure elections everywhere. The Brennan Center for Justice’s research confirmed that voter fraud is a myth (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/debunking-voter-fraud-myth). Even the conservative Heritage Foundation could only find 71 instances (https://electionfraud.heritage.org/search?case_type=All&fraud_type=All&state=CA) of voter fraud in California — over more than four decades. Also, California already takes election integrity (https://abc7news.com/post/150000-mail-ballots-rejected-californias-primary-despite-efforts-count-every-vote/19571066/) seriously, which is one reason our process of confirming elections is so slow (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/17/upshot/california-slow-election-results.html).
RELATED: Endorsement Cheat Sheet: Mercury News and East Bay Times Editorial Boards’ top picks for California’s Nov. 3 general election (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/13/bay-area-news-group-california-election-endorsements-november-2026/)
Our editorial board repeatedly asked the Yes on Prop. 39 campaign for evidence of voter fraud in California, rampant or otherwise, and they deflected, dodged and denied the premise of our questions. They insisted that fraud wasn’t actually the issue — that Prop. 39 is about improving public trust and confidence in our democracy.
So it’s purely coincidence that Donald Trump demanded “voter ID” laws in California as a condition for wildfire disaster relief (https://abc7.com/post/president-donald-trump-wants-voter-id-laws-condition-aid-california/15833908/) last year. Or that the measure’s biggest backer, Illinois billionaire Richard Uihlein, has a history ofcontributing (https://www.propublica.org/article/uline-uihlein-election-denial) to the campaigns of election deniers.
According to the Public Policy Institute of California (https://data.ddhq.io/polls/2026/05/30/Public-Policy-Institute-of-California-California), a quarter of likely voters are very concerned that it’s too easy for ineligible people to vote. That’s not zero, but it also doesn’t mean we should be changing election laws to accommodate the fact-free fears of a minority of Californians.
In other polls about trust in our elections, it is overwhelmingly Republicans who are the most concerned. That’s fine. But if they really cared about improving those numbers, we’d recommend they start by asking the president to stop spreading false information.
We absolutely wouldn’t recommend, as Prop. 39 does, that private citizens be allowed to sue if they believe the government isn’t complying with the measure’s rules. We don’t even want to imagine the kind of frivolous litigation that could inspire.
Why panic?
It’s possible to view Prop. 39 and say, “What’s the big deal?” Thirty-six statesrequire (https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_identification_laws_by_state) voters to present identification before voting in person.
Well, the big deal is that a lot of eligible people might not be able to vote if the measure is passed. Millions of Californians (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/Who%20Lacks%20ID%20and%20Proof%20of%20Citizenship%20in%20California%20Today_.pdf) wouldn’t have the ID required to satisfy this proposal. (They’d have to request a new one.) And, as the No on Prop. 39 campaign pointed out to us, when Texas implemented similar mail-ballot ID rules, rejections shot up (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/) from 1% to 12%.
Plus, completely revamping the voter verification system will come with financial costs — “between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year,” according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Prop. 39 isn’t just about voter ID. It contains a provision that is deeply problematic: requiring election officials to use their “best efforts” to verify the citizenship status of voters they register, with regular audits to ensure compliance.
But there is no reliable government list of U.S. citizens. The Supreme Court decided that the federal government could continue to try to create one, but it’s already full of mistakes (https://www.npr.org/2026/09/25/nx-s1-5976804/supreme-court-trump-save-noncitizen-voting), labeling many citizens as ineligible to vote.
This deeply flawed measure would create chaos for no reason.
Reject Prop. 39.
(Editor’s note: To read our other recommendations for California’s Nov. 3 General Election, please visit mercurynews.com/endorsements (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/13/bay-area-news-group-california-election-endorsements-november-2026/).)

I have a very thorough picture now. Let me confirm a few last points:

1. Whether the Yes campaign has acknowledged the absence of a cure provision, and whether the East Bay Times Q&A (Nov 2) claim about a cure process contradicts the text. Already confirmed: the text has no cure provision; the AG says ballots are "invalidated"; the Yes campaign claims it "allows a 'curring' process" — this is not in the text.

2. Whether the measure would slow counting. SF Chronicle reported experts say it would slow down, not speed up, vote-counting.

3. Whether the Yes campaign's claim about "100,000 signature mismatch rejections" is false — confirmed: 71,387 statewide in Nov 2024.

4. Funding: 80.3% of Yes money from out-of-state donors; Richard Uihlein (Wisconsin) $17M = 51.6%; Joseph Gebbia $8M = 24.3%. So two out-of-state-ish billionaires = ~76% of the Yes campaign. Note Gebbia is Airbnb co-founder (California-based? he's listed as Samara). Uihlein is Wisconsin.

Actually the opposition's "MAGA billionaires" claim is partially supported (Uihlein is a major Trump/mega-donor; Luckey family connection), though the Yes campaign disputes Trump's direct involvement. But note: the "bipartisan" framing is undermined by the fact that 80% of funding is from out-of-state donors, and all major political endorsers are Republicans.

5. The Huntington Beach precedent: courts blocked Huntington Beach's voter-approved voter ID charter amendment, and the CA Supreme Court declined review in Jan 2026. Reason: state law (Elections Code §10005, SB 1174) bars cities from requiring voter ID. Prop 39 would put it in the state constitution, overriding that.

6. Important legal risk: the measure is "self-executing" but leaves critical terms undefined. This creates chaos risk — a constitutional amendment that takes effect on the 5th day after certification, requiring ID at "any election in the State," while the Legislature hasn't defined which IDs qualify. And every citizen can sue over compliance. That's a serious governance risk: it invites litigation over every election.

Let me do one more round of research on:
- The Mercury News/Bay Area News Group endorsement (No) reasoning.
- Whether there's any evidence about how many Californians lack qualifying ID, and specifically the burden on the ~22 million existing registrants needing to re-designate.
- The SF Chronicle article on whether it would slow counting.
- Any final polling.

Actually, I think I have enough. Let me do a couple more targeted searches to make sure I'm not missing a strong pro argument or new development (e.g., a court ruling on the substance, or a compromise).

Let me check: (a) any post-election-day developments? No, election is Nov 3, 2026 and today appears to be ~Nov 2-3, 2026. (b) The Mercury News endorsement. (c) The SF Chronicle counting article.

Let me also verify the UCLA Voting Rights Project opposition and any expert consensus.

One more important angle: does Prop 39 conflict with federal law (HAVA) for mail voters? HAVA §301(b) requires first-time mail registrants to provide ID, but states can be stricter. However, requiring ID numbers on envelopes for ALL mail voters could conflict with... actually no federal preemption issue there. But there's a potential issue with UOCAVA/military overseas voters — the text explicitly directs the Legislature to handle that "consistent with federal law."

Another potential issue: the Americans with Disabilities Act / Section 203 language assistance, and voters with disabilities who can't easily write 4 digits. Also blind voters.

Let me do final searches.

Would Prop 39 speed up or slow down California’s vote-counting?
By Sara DiNatale (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/sara-dinatale/) , Staff Writer Oct 11, 2026
Marion Gautier helps organize and count absentee and mail-in ballots at the San Francisco Department of Elections at City Hall on Nov. 6, 2019.
Gabrielle Lurie/S.F. Chronicle
Most of the conservatives who critique California’s election system have two separate complaints: They believe California’s vote-counting process is riddled with fraud, and they think the state takes far too long to count its votes. (Many say that the latter is evidence of the former.)
Backers of Proposition 39, a measure to implement voter ID requirements, say their plan will solve both issues. Experts, however, say the measure’s requirements would slow down, not speed up, vote-counting.
Chronicle endorsements: Editorial Board’s recommendations for 2026 election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 39 would require voters to show government-issued identification each time they cast a ballot in person. People who vote by mail would have to register a PIN that’s either the last four digits of their Social Security number or their driver’s license number. They could also request a free “voter ID” with a number on it. The number would need to be handwritten on the ballot envelope. Election offices would then have to check and verify the number. Critics say that means essentially 26 million people would have to reregister to vote across California.
The proposition’s cocreator, Assembly Member Carl DeMaio, R-San Diego, has cast Prop 39 as a simple and necessary change to fortify voters’ trust in state elections. During a May episode of his podcast, DeMaio said the measure’s requirement of a four-digit PIN would replace the signature verification process for the more than 80% of voters using mail-in ballots. He said that if Prop 39 becomes law, mail-in ballots would be processed “literally within 48 hours of them coming back.”
Meredith Shields, the press secretary for the Yes on 39 campaign, reiterated those claims in a statement on Friday, saying “providing a four-digit PIN when voting by mail, election officials will not have to match electronic signatures.”
But the measure does not contain any language about the PIN numbers usurping signature verification, which is codified in state law. That means the new handwritten PINs would be required and verified in addition to signatures, not in lieu of them, voting experts said.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The state’s official voter guide lays out what a yes vote means: “Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote” — language that suggests the PIN is an extra layer of verification, not a replacement.
“Voters can read the language of Prop 39 for themselves,” said Brittany Stonesifer, an attorney and voting rights advocate with nonprofit California Common Cause. “It would add additional requirements for mail ballots. It says nothing about removing the existing signature verification process.”
DeMaio suggested during his podcast that there would be a “scanning” system for the PIN numbers, but that would require infrastructure and technology that election offices don’t yet have.
“The notion that this will speed up the process is asinine,” said Stephen Richer, a Republican former recorder of Maricopa County, Ariz. “I don’t know how having an additional requirement could possibly make the process go faster.”
Richer said he broadly supports ID checks at polling places to verify that the person trying to vote matches the person recorded in the voter rolls. California doesn’t do that. Voters must present a government ID when they register to vote, but when voting in person they only must provide poll workers with their name and address, and sign a voter roster.

“It would absolutely result in valid mail ballots being rejected, potentially at a high level, with no evidence that it would increase security,” Stonesifer said of the four-digit PIN numbers.
Assembly Member Gail Pellerin, D-Santa Cruz, who is the head of the Assembly Elections Committee and a former elections official, agrees. She told the Los Angeles Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/newsletter/2026-09-28/skelton-monday-politics-newsletter-voter-id) that under Prop 39, not only would some voters’ ballots be rejected by mistake but the measure would “absolutely” slow down counting.
Richer, Stonesifer, Pellerin and other voting experts largely agree signature verification is a secure and efficient way to vet mail-in ballots. Some election offices use software to quickly confirm a signature match and kick any questionable ones to workers who can pull up someone’s state signature history to see how it may have changed over time.
If the signature still looks odd, they notify the voter it needs to be fixed. California has a long window allowing ballot curing, which is a common criticism of the state’s lagging vote-tallying process. But legislation just signed into law by Gov. Gavin Newsom requires all counties to allow digital signature curing in order to speed the process.
Shields, the Prop 39 campaign spokesperson, said the measure would not only speed the process, but would conserve resources.

“When Prop 39 passes, IDs will be free of charge and the verification and counting of ballots will be faster, more accurate, and will save election officials valuable time and resources,” she said.
The state’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, however, estimates the measure would cost the state and local governments tens of millions to hundreds of millions of dollars. Darius Kemp, the director of Common Cause California, said the measure would also take resources away from counties and clerks, impeding them from counting more quickly.
Pamela Smith, president of Verified Voting, a nonprofit focused on election security, said that if someone was so determined to cheat that they would spoof a signature, there’s no reason to believe they wouldn’t also pilfer a PIN. She, too, was wary that the measure would speed up the count.
“The costs to taxpayers associated with implementation are significant, which might not matter if this were a game changer for efficiency or security, but it is neither,” Smith said.
Prop 39 does not include a curing process for PIN codes.

“My mother has very interesting handwriting,” Rep. Lateefah Simon, D-Oakland, said during a Friday rally against Prop 39. “If, in fact, the registrar of voters cannot read her handwriting or her Social Security number ... what will happen to her ballot? It will be discarded.”
State Sen. Jesse Arreguín, D-Berkeley, also argued the measure will impede in-person voting.
“Repetitive ID checks under Prop 39 are not only unnecessary, they will slow our checking and create longer lines and delays for people to vote and make it harder for them to participate in their right to vote,” Arreguín said during the Friday rally in Oakland.
Stonesifer said funding more staffers in election offices — rather than implementing a new system to scan four-digit codes — would be a better way to speed up the counting process.
DeMaio and his critics do agree on one thing: They’re all encouraging voters to return their ballots early. One of the biggest factors that slows California’s tabulation is the surge of vote-by-mail ballots returned on Election Day.

In requiring voters to show IDs before receiving their ballots (among other restrictive voting rules and audits), it gives credence to President Donald Trump’s longstanding and repeatedly debunked claims that millions of noncitizens routinely vote in U.S. elections.

Manufactured crisis
Multiple groups have studied the issue and found scant evidence of widespread fraud. The California State Library (https://www.library.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/crb-reports/CRB-Voter-Fraud-Presentation-Senate-Elections-2026-04-03.pdf) looked at 14 counties where grand juries issued reports on the risk of voter fraud in the 2020, 2022 and 2024 elections and found secure elections everywhere. **1. The main benefit being advertised is not in the measure.** DeMaio and the Yes campaign say the four-digit PIN *replaces* signature matching. It doesn't — Prop 39 never repeals Elections Code §3019. The Secretary of State's own guide says a yes vote means voters provide "**additional** identifying information." Common Cause, Loyola election-law scholars, former Maricopa County recorder Stephen Richer (R), Assembly Elections Chair Gail Pellerin (a former registrar), and Verified Voting all agree: mail voters get **two** independent ways to be rejected instead of one. Even *Reason*, which is sympathetic to voter ID, says it would "no doubt burden our excruciatingly slow ballot counting."

**2. There is no cure process — for a brand-new failure point.** Today, a signature problem triggers a strong statutory safety net: a presumption your signature is valid, "an exact match is not required," rejection only if two extra officials each find a mismatch "beyond a reasonable doubt," notice by mail plus call/text/email, and ~22 days to fix it. Prop 39 has **no cure provision at all**. The AG's official summary says the ballot is simply "invalidated" — write your driver's license number when you designated your SSN and your vote doesn't count. Yet on Nov. 2 the Yes campaign told the East Bay Times it "allows a 'curring' process if a voter transposes numbers." That promise exists only in a press quote, not in the constitution they're asking you to ratify. Texas is the cautionary case: after its 2021 mail-ballot ID law, rejections went from under 1% to **over 12%** — roughly 1 in 8 votes invalidated — and a peer-reviewed study found turnout fell.

**3. The pro argument's central statistic is false, and a judge already ruled against this campaign twice.** The ballot argument claims "more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches" in the last election. SOS data: **71,387** statewide in Nov. 2024 (43,976 in June 2026). Separately, Judge Shelleyanne Chang found the proponents' claims that Prop 39 makes voting "easier," protects privacy, and "saves millions" to be **false and misleading** — writing that the measure actually makes ID numbers "less private, and less secure," and that savings claims were "objectively untrue." They were forced to rewrite their argument. Judge Jennifer Rockwell then upheld the AG's title — "**Prohibits** citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification" — rejecting the campaign's own insistence that it bars nobody from voting, because "vote" plainly includes the counting. When a measure's sponsors lose both of their own lawsuits over how it's described, that's information.

**4. The citizenship-verification mandate can't be executed.** There is no comprehensive government list of U.S. citizens. Federal databases track the immigration status of the foreign-born — not the birthright citizenship of the ~90% of Americans born here. That's why E-Verify has been resisted for decades and why courts have repeatedly blocked comparable mandates. The risk runs at eligible citizens being wrongly flagged and purged. Notably, the **San Diego Union-Tribune** — in DeMaio's own region, and a board that says "what's the big deal?" about in-person ID in 36 other states — still recommends no on this ground alone: "the records needed to do it accurately don't exist."

**5. The problem is tiny; the exposure is enormous.** The California State Library reviewed grand jury reports from 14 counties covering 2020–2024 and found **no evidence of systemic or significant fraud**. The Heritage Foundation — the conservative think tank behind Project 2025 — documents just **71** California voter-fraud cases across 1982–2025, all prosecuted. Brookings: "no election outcome in the US has ever been altered by ballot fraud." Against that: 13 million mail ballots per presidential cycle and roughly **22 million existing registrants** who would each have to affirmatively re-designate an ID (the LAO confirms this applies to "new and existing voters"; the Budget & Policy Center says it "effectively means" re-registering) in a state where 80%+ vote by mail. A 2026 University of Maryland analysis found ~2.7 million Californians (11% of eligible voters) have no driver's license, another 13% hold one that's expired or has a stale address or name, and 3+ million would struggle to produce citizenship documents — with people of color, young, disabled, low-income, and married women who changed names overrepresented. And you'd be writing the last four of a government ID — possibly an SSN — on the *outside* of an envelope next to your name, address, and signature, when Gov. Code §7924.000 currently keeps those numbers strictly confidential.

### The strongest case for yes, and why it falls short

It's real and I don't want to strawman it. Voter ID is popular in the abstract; 36 states have some form, as do Canada and Mexico. California verifies 80%+ of voters by handwriting judgment applied unevenly across 58 counties. Our rolls do carry stale records, ballots do get mailed to people who've moved, and ballot harvesting has genuine abuse potential. The ID is free, mail voting and extended hours survive, and a former Republican Secretary of State, Bill Jones, supports it. Aggregate research (a 2019 NBER review; *Research & Politics*, Dec. 2024) finds strict ID laws have minimal net turnout effects.

But none of that rescues **this drafting**. Add a private right of action letting anyone sue any of 58 counties over undefined compliance duties and you get what Loyola's Justin Levitt called a "generic litigation trap" and the Chronicle called "CEQA for voting rights" — permanent litigation cloud over every result. Put it in the constitution as self-executing with the operative terms blank, and the errors are much harder to fix than a statute's: correcting them later takes another statewide vote or a two-thirds legislative amendment that "furthers the purposes of the act." The LAO prices it at tens of millions to low hundreds of millions **every year**. And the "bipartisan" framing doesn't survive the finance reports: Richard Uihlein of Wisconsin gave $17M (51.6%) and Joseph Gebbia $8M (24.3%) — two donors, ~76% of the money — with **80.3% of Yes funds from outside California**, and every major political endorser a Republican. PPIC found 85% of Republicans and 19% of Democrats in favor. The measure polled competitively in September, then fell to 37–41% yes in the final PPIC, Berkeley IGS, and Citrin/Politico surveys as voters learned the details — which is what you'd expect when the specifics are worse than the slogan.

Finally, the trust rationale is undercut by the proponents' own data: PPIC shows confidence in how California counts votes **rose** from 47% to 63% among likely voters between 2017 and 2024. And multiple studies find strict ID laws barely move voter confidence, because confidence tracks partisanship and whether your candidate won. When the Mercury News board repeatedly asked the Yes campaign for evidence of fraud, they report the campaign "deflected, dodged and denied the premise."

Editorial boards: **No** — SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee/McClatchy, San Diego Union-Tribune, Mercury News/East Bay Times, Santa Cruz Sentinel. **Yes** — OC Register, LA Daily News. Opposed by the CMA, ACLU, Common Cause, League of Women Voters, and the UCLA Voting Rights Project.

**Vote no.** If you want election-integrity reform, the durable route is statutory: fund county election offices, let counties join the multistate voter-roll accuracy consortium they've been requesting, tighten who may collect ballots, and require counting to begin the day ballots are mailed. That addresses the legitimate concerns without entrenching an undefined, cure-less mandate in the state constitution.

**Proposition 39**, also known as the **California voter ID initiative**, is an initiated constitutional amendment in the state of California that on November 3, 2026, will be on the ballot.

Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Voter Identification
Registered Voter List Administration Initiative
Summary
Proposition 39 began as a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment filed with the California Attorney General's (https://oag.ca.gov/) office on July 16, 2025. The initiative received a revised ballot title and was approved for signature gathering on September 19, 2025. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 874,641 valid signatures.The campaign submitted nearly 1.37 million signatures on March 2, 2026 and the initiative officially qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 39 on April 24, 2026.
On July 27, 2026, Californians for Voter ID (https://www.voteridca.org/) filed a lawsuit against the Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/) challenging the new ballot title for Proposition 39, which was drafted by Attorney General Rob Bonta after his office received the amendment. The plaintiffs argued that the new title of “prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification,” was false and misleading, as it did not include the original title’s reference to additional voter identification and citizenship verification requirements. The Attorney General’s Office maintained that the revised language more accurately describes the measure’s provisions. On August 6, 2026, Sacramento County Superior Court found for the state and ruled that the ballot title is sufficient, thus the measure will remain on the ballot unchanged.
Proposition 39 would establish new identification and citizenship-verification requirements for California elections. State and local election officials would be required to make “best efforts,” using government records, to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually on the percentage verified in each county. Voters would also have to select a government-issued form of identification when registering in order to vote by mail, and the state would provide a free voter identification card to anyone who requests one.
The measure would also require voters to provide identifying information each time they cast a ballot. In-person voters would need to present government-issued identification, while mail voters would provide the last four digits of their selected identification number on the ballot envelope for verification. Elections officials would confirm that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information. The State Auditor would review state and county compliance every odd numbered year. Proposition 39 mandates that the Legislature would need to clarify details not included in the proposition and they would have to pass additional laws before the measure could be fully implemented.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs by an estimated tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars annually, although the exact amount would depend on how the measure is implemented. These costs amount to less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Major costs would be influenced by decisions about the new voter identification card, administrative requirements, and the number of voters requesting cards. As ineligible voters or eligible voters lack the required identification are removed from voting, some savings could result.
What your vote means
YES: A "yes" vote supports amending the state constitution to require government-issued ID for in-person voting or the last four digits of a designated government ID for mail-in voting, mandate annual citizenship-verification reporting for county voter rolls, and require odd-year compliance audits by the State Auditor.
NO: A "no" vote opposes these changes, maintaining current law where government ID is not required to vote, and voters attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury without requiring election officials to verify attestations against government data or report verification rates.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters of Proposition 39 argue that requiring voter identification would strengthen confidence in California elections by adding safeguards they believe are currently lacking. They point to voter ID requirements in other states and countries as evidence that such rules are a common feature of democratic election systems rather than an unusual restriction. Supporters also contend that changes such as universal mail ballots and ballot collection have increased the need for additional identity checks. While they do not necessarily claim that widespread voter fraud is occurring, they maintain that Proposition 39 would make the election process more secure, transparent, and less vulnerable to public doubt.
Opponents of Proposition 39 argue that the measure would impose unnecessary barriers on eligible voters without addressing a demonstrated problem in California elections. They contend that existing procedures already provide multiple safeguards for verifying voters and that additional identification and citizenship checks could lead to eligible ballots being rejected, with disproportionate effects on people with disabilities and others who may have difficulty meeting the new requirements.
Critics also raise privacy concerns about placing partial identification numbers on mail ballot envelopes and argue that implementing the measure would create significant new administrative costs. Finally, opponents characterize Proposition 39 as part of a national push for stricter voting rules that they believe would make voting more difficult rather than meaningfully improve election security.

Endorsement: Prop 39 would create CEQA for voting rights. No thanks
Even if you think voter fraud is a problem in California (it’s not), Prop 39 would turn our elections into a never-ending lawsuit
Proposition 39 would require Californians to present or incorporate some form of identification when voting. It is almost certain to disenfranchise eligible voters. The Chronicle’s editorial board recommends a no vote.
Todd Trumbull/S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 12, 2026
Is voter fraud rampant in California?
A May poll by the Public Policy Institute of California (https://data.ddhq.io/polls/2026/05/30/Public-Policy-Institute-of-California-California) found that 41% of likely voters here were either “very” or “somewhat” concerned that it’s too easy for ineligible voters to cast ballots.
That’s not an insignificant number.

So, how can California shore up trust?
Carl DeMaio, the firebrand Republican Assembly member from San Diego, claims to have the answer: Proposition 39 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
The measure would create a host of new voter-identification requirements in California and mandate regular election audits. Prop 39 was placed on the November ballot via a signature-gathering effort by volunteers from DeMaio’s advocacy organization (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/02/carl-demaio-california-maga-voter-id-prop-39-01103730?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e), Reform California, and paid operatives funded by Julie Luckey (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2025/11/24/the-donor-powering-a-voter-id-push-in-california-00667090), whose son Palmer was recently named as a leader of the Trump administration’s new Project Meridian war council (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/pentagon-weapon-military-war-22464710.php).
Even though wealthy out-of-state Republicans have largely funded the yes campaign, DeMaio inexplicably insisted to the editorial board that the measure is “a balanced, bipartisan approach.”

Article continues below this ad
Prop 39 is “the best way to shut down the conspiracy theories that irresponsible politicians spread,” DeMaio said.
Well, no.
The best way is for those irresponsible politicians, paramount among them DeMaio’s ally, President Donald Trump, to stop sowing unfounded disbelief.
Because by every available measure, California’s voting system is working.
The California State Library’s research bureau examined reports from 14 counties (https://www.library.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/crb-reports/CRB-Voter-Fraud-Presentation-Senate-Elections-2026-04-03.pdf) where grand juries investigated voter fraud risks from 2020 to 2024 and found an overwhelming consensus: no evidence of systemic or significant fraud. Even the right-wing Heritage Foundation — the organization behind Project 2025 — identified just 71 instances of known voter fraud in California (https://electionfraud.heritage.org/search?case_type=All&fraud_type=All&state=CA) from 1982 to 2025.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
All of those cases were prosecuted — evidence that California takes election integrity seriously. In fact, the state rejected its highest percentage of mail ballots in more than a decade (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-mail-ballot-rejections-22359196.php) for the June 2 primary — largely because they were postmarked after Election Day or arrived too late. There was also an uptick in signatures that election officials couldn’t verify.
Yet Prop 39 supporters insist on the need for additional identity verification.
To understand Prop 39’s proposed changes and the impact, let’s first look at the state’s existing processes:
Under California law (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration), anyone registering to vote must prove their identity via their driver’s license, state identification number or the last four digits of their Social Security number. Election officials check this identification against state and federal databases. Voters must also attest under penalty of perjury — which carries a potential prison sentence — that they’re a U.S. citizen living in California who’s at least 18 years old and not currently in prison or found incapable of voting by a court.
Every registered voter in California then receives a mail-in ballot, which most residents prefer (more than 80% voted this way in the past election). Before counting it, election officials check whether the voter’s signature on the outside of the ballot matches the signature on file (usually from a driver’s license). If it doesn’t, election officials give voters a chance to “cure” it by notifying them of the issue and providing a correction form (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2026-general/november-3-2026-general-combo-statement.pdf), which they have 22 days to return.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
People voting in person typically don’t have to present ID, but they do have to sign a registration list at the polls.
Prop 39 would change all that. To vote by mail, Californians would have to preselect a form of government-issued identification and write the last four digits of that ID on the outside of their ballot.
To vote in person, Californians would need to show a government-issued ID. Prop 39 mandates the state provide free “voter identification cards” — which do not currently exist — to those who request them. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop39-110326.pdf) estimated that creating these cards, in addition to other expenses resulting from Prop 39, could cost local and state governments hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
The measure also requires state and local elections officials to employ “best efforts” to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens and to publish annual reports revealing the percentage of verified voters. It mandates the state auditor to review compliance every other year.
What forms of government-issued ID would be acceptable under Prop 39, and how would voters preselect the ID they want to use for their 4-digit PIN? Do they get a chance to cure their ballots if they write the wrong digits on their vote-by-mail envelope? And what would be considered “best efforts” to verify someone’s citizenship status — given that even the federal government doesn’t have a comprehensive list of citizens?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 39 directs the state Legislature to “promptly” enact laws to answer these questions. It also creates a private right of action that permits any person who believes state or local government isn’t complying with the measure to take those entities to court.
Justin Levitt, a constitutional and election law expert at the Loyola Law School, called this a “generic litigation trap” that opens the door to countless frivolous lawsuits.
Just as the California Environmental Quality Act enables aggrieved NIMBYs to weaponize the legal system against development projects they dislike, Prop 39 will do the same with elections.
“You will have plenty of advocacy organizations that are eager to sue over perceived noncompliance with this initiative early and often,” Levitt told the editorial board.
And Prop 39 is almost certain to disenfranchise eligible voters.
Large numbers of California U.S. citizens lack either IDs or proof of citizenship. A 2026 University of Maryland analysis (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/Who%20Lacks%20ID%20and%20Proof%20of%20Citizenship%20in%20California%20Today_.pdf) found that about 2.7 million Californians, or about 11% of eligible voters, don’t have a driver’s license, while 13% have one that’s expired or has an outdated address or name. People of color, young residents, disabled Californians and lower-income residents are disproportionately represented in these groups.
The study also found 24% of Californians don’t have a passport and that more than 3 million voting-age Californians would have difficulty readily accessing documents proving their citizenship.
In short, Prop 39 would do little to stop the minimal fraud that exists while creating millions “more chances for valid ballots to be rejected,” Abdi Soltani, executive director of ACLU of Northern California, told the editorial board.
After Texas passed a similar voter-ID law in 2021, its rate of rejected ballots skyrocketed from less than 1% to more than 12% (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/), effectively invalidating 1 in 8 votes cast in the 2022 primary. A peer-reviewed study (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/737439) found it also reduced voter turnout in subsequent elections.

California could do more to assuage concerns about election integrity. Counties have been begging the state for permission to join a nonprofit, multistate organization that helps officials improve the accuracy of their voter rolls (https://apcp.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2024-04/ab-2050-pellerin-apcp-analysis_1.pdf).

Excellent, very substantive. Now let me check a few more things:

1. The CalMatters voter guide for a nonpartisan summary.
2. The California Budget & Policy Center issue brief on how many voters would be affected.
3. The strongest case FOR: the "pro" side arguments and the Daily News editorial endorsement, plus any Republican/conservative analysis. Also whether there's a legitimate concern: declining trust in elections, 41% concerned.
4. Whether the measure has a cure process — important. Let me confirm from the LAO report and text. The text has no explicit cure provision. That's a serious drafting flaw.
5. Federal law issues: e.g., would this conflict with UOCAVA/military overseas voting? The text says the Legislature shall "provide for voting by military and overseas voters consistent with federal law" — so that's addressed.
6. Whether the citizenship verification requirement would be problematic — there's no comprehensive federal database of citizens. The "best efforts" is vague.

Let me also check the LAO PDF for more detail and the CalMatters guide.

Let me also consider: is there a legitimate "yes" argument? Voter ID is popular; other democracies require ID. But this specific measure is unusually strict and poorly drafted for a mail-ballot state. Key concerns:
- No cure process specified for mail ballots (unlike current signature cure).
- Requires voters to pre-designate an ID type in their registration record; existing voters who haven't done this "may not get a mail ballot at all" per the opposition argument. Actually let's check: the text says "The type of identification designated by each voter must be indicated in their voter registration record, noted on the mail ballot envelope provided to them, and available to them on request by phone or electronically." And AG title says "Prohibits voting by mail unless voter designates a government-issued identification number for their voter registration." So ~22 million existing registered voters would need to take an affirmative new step to designate an ID type before they can receive/count a mail ballot. That's a massive one-time administrative burden on the entire electorate in a state where 80%+ vote by mail. The LAO doesn't quantify but it's a big deal.
- Privacy: last 4 digits of SSN on the outside of an envelope that passes through the mail and many hands; ballot envelopes become part of election records potentially subject to public records requests. Let me verify whether CA ballot envelopes are public records. Under Elections Code § 3025 / Gov Code, "signature verification envelopes" — hmm. Actually, California law: Elections Code § 2166 et seq. deals with voter registration confidentiality. Ballot envelopes are retained by county elections officials for 22 months and are... I recall that some states treat them as public records. Let me search to verify this claim.

Actually, let me be careful not to overstate. Let me search for whether California ballot return envelopes are subject to the Public Records Act.

7. Also worth checking: does the measure conflict with the state constitution's free elections clause, and has anyone predicted litigation? The Chronicle's Levitt "generic litigation trap" quote covers that.

8. Let me also check the CalMatters guide and the Budget Center brief for numbers on who lacks ID.

Let me do a few searches in parallel.

Proposition 39
Require identification for voting
This initiative would require voters to show government-issued identification at the polls and order election officials to verify that all registered voters are U.S. citizens. Voters who cast a mail-in ballot would need to give the last four digits of a government ID, such as a driver’s license number. California currently requires residents to provide an identification card and Social Security number to register to vote, but does not request it at polling places. It was placed on the ballot by conservative groups.

Summary
Support
Supporters argue that ID requirements at voting sites will strengthen voters’ trust in California’s election process, and that most states require voters to show some form of identification to vote.
Oppose
Opponents say requiring ID will make it harder for eligible voters who don’t have a driver’s license or other supporting documents to vote. They say this will disproportionately affect those with disabilities, who are low-income or have recently moved.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Proposition 39 on the November ballot would impose unnecessary, harmful, and costly new identification (ID) requirements on millions of California voters. It would harm US citizens by making it harder for them to vote, exposing them to identity theft, and putting them at risk of being erroneously removed from voter rolls. Prop. 39 is part of broader national efforts to create new barriers to voting, which primarily impact people with low incomes, young people, and people of color, limiting Californians’ say in how public tax dollars are raised and spent.

Prop. 39 Is Part of a Nationwide Effort to Restrict Voting and Limit People’s Say in Policymaking

What Would Prop. 39 Do?
Prop. 39 would amend California’s Constitution to add new voter ID requirements that would affect current and future voters. The measure would also impose new responsibilities on state and local officials related to election administration. Specifically, Prop. 39:
Requires Elections Officials to “Use Best Efforts” to Verify Every Registered Voter’s Citizenship Status
Current Law
Californians are required (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voting-resources/voting-california/who-can-vote-california) to be US citizens to vote. 1 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 2101(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=2101.). There are two exceptions: Oakland and San Francisco allow certain noncitizens to vote in local school board elections. To register to vote, a person must declare in writing, under penalty of perjury, that they meet all voter eligibility requirements, including that they are a US citizen (https://covr.sos.ca.gov/). 2 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 2150(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=2150.). Under federal law (https://www.justice.gov/crt/national-voter-registration-act-1993-nvra), state motor vehicle agencies — like California’s Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) — must provide residents with the opportunity to register to vote when they apply for or renew a driver’s license or state ID card and/or change their address. In California, this is known as Motor Voter (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/california-motor-voter/frequently-asked-questions). DMV customers who indicate that they are eligible to vote are registered to vote by the Secretary of State (SOS) unless they opt out. However, the DMV does not send to the SOS (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/california-motor-voter/frequently-asked-questions) information regarding customers who indicate they are not eligible to vote. Falsely claiming to be a US citizen on a voter registration application and attempting to vote would expose a person to state felony charges as well as the possibility of deportation under federal law. 3 (javascript:void(0)) For example, see California Elections Code, Section 18560(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=18560.), 8 U.S.C. Section 1227(a)(6)(a) (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title8-section1227&num=0&edition=prelim), and 18 U.S.C. Section 611 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/611).
In addition, state law makes it a crime to:
Vote or attempt to vote more than once in an election,
Impersonate or attempt to impersonate a voter in an election, or
Apply for or cast a vote-by-mail ballot by fraudulently signing the name of a fake person, another qualified voter, or a person who is not qualified to vote. 4 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 18560(b)-(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=18560.) and Section 18578 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=18578.).
A person who is convicted of any of these crimes could be imprisoned for up to three years.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require state and county election officials to “use best efforts” to verify, using “government data,” that registered voters are US citizens. The measure does not define “best efforts” or what constitutes “government data.” In addition, election officials would have to annually report the share of registered voters in each county whose citizenship status has been verified.
Requires Voters to Present Additional Identifying Information When They Cast Their Ballot
Current Law
All states, including California, already have voter ID requirements (https://electionlab.mit.edu/research/voter-identification) as required by federal law (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/hava-id-standards). For example, to register to vote, Californians must provide (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) a California driver’s license or state ID number or the last four digits of their Social Security Number (SSN) if they lack a driver’s license or ID card. Californians who lack a driver’s license, a state ID card, or a SSN are assigned a unique identifier (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) to validate their registration. Californians generally are not required (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) to present an ID when voting. 5 (javascript:void(0)) Californians may need to show (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) an acceptable form of ID when they vote by mail or in person if all of the following apply: 1) they’re voting for the first time in a federal election, 2) they registered by mail or online, and 3) they did not provide a California ID or SSN when registering. Acceptable forms of ID (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/hava-id-standards) include, but aren’t limited to, a California driver’s license or state ID card, a US passport, a student or military ID, a utility bill, and a bank statement.
When voting by mail, California voters sign the outside of their ballot envelope, and elections officials verify the signature before counting the ballot. 6 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 3011(a)(7) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=3011.) and Section 3019 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=3019.). Voters must be given an opportunity to correct or “cure” their ballot if they failed to sign the envelope or if their signature does not match the signature on file. 7 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Sections 3019(c)-(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=3019.).
When voting in person, California voters state their name and address and sign a list of registered voters under penalty of perjury. 8 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 14216(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=14216.). While election officials do not verify (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm) the signatures of in-person voters before counting their ballots, counties have procedures in place to prevent voter fraud. 9 (javascript:void(0)) For example, in many counties, poll workers are able to look up voting records in real time to ensure that a voter has not already cast a ballot in the election. This applies to counties that participate (https://www.sos.ca.gov/voters-choice-act/vca-participating-counties) in California’s Voter’s Choice Act (https://www.sos.ca.gov/voters-choice-act) as well as to counties that have adopted the Sign, Scan, and Go (https://www.placercountyelections.gov/sign-scan-go/) option. As noted above, it is a crime in California to fraudulently vote in an election, to vote more than once, or to impersonate another voter. Penalties range from up to one year in a county jail to up to three years in state prison.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would impose new requirements on Californians to cast a ballot in person or mail a ballot.
To vote in person:
Voters would have to present a “government-issued” ID when they arrive at their polling place. Prop. 39 does not specifically define what “government-issued” ID means, so the Legislature would need to clarify which types of ID a voter could present to prove their identity. 10 (javascript:void(0)) Prop. 39 says broadly that “government-issued” ID “means documentation that allows conclusive verification of the voter’s identity.”
To vote by mail:
All new and existing voters would have to select a “government-issued” ID that would be reflected in their “voter registration record.” This requirement effectively means that people who are currently registered to vote would have to re-register to provide their chosen ID to election officials.
When voting, voters would have to write on the outside of their ballot envelope the last four digits of a “unique identifying number” from the “government-issued” ID that they selected for the purpose of voting. 11 (javascript:void(0)) The government-issued ID that voters choose for this purpose would have to subsequently be made available to them “on request by phone or electronically.”
Election officials would verify that the four digits written on the envelope match the last four digits of the ID number in the voter’s registration record.
Requires the State to Create a New Voter ID Card
Current Law
California currently allows Californians to apply for three types of ID cards (https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/driver-licenses-identification-cards/identification-id-cards/) in addition to drivers’ licenses that are used to prove identity or age. 12 (javascript:void(0)) The ID cards are issued by the California Department of Motor Vehicles as alternatives to a driver’s license and cannot be used to operate a motor vehicle.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require the state to provide a voter ID card to eligible voters who request one. Voters could use this optional ID as their “government-issued” ID for voting by mail or in person. This card would be provided to voters free of charge.
Requires Ongoing State Audits of How the State and Counties Are Complying with Prop. 39
Current Law
California’s independently elected (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/california-state-constitutional-offices-defined/) Secretary of State oversees (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/about-agency) all elections in the state, including ensuring election laws are enforced, testing and approving voting equipment, compiling election returns, and certifying election results.
In addition, California’s independent, nonpartisan State Auditor (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/about-us/) conducts performance audits and investigations of various state and local government agencies and recommends solutions for improving services. However, the State Auditor currently does not have a formal, ongoing role in auditing California’s elections or evaluating election administration.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require the State Auditor, in odd-numbered years, to audit state and county compliance with Prop. 39 and report any recommendations for improvement.
Requires the State Legislature to Pass Laws to Implement Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require the Legislature to “promptly enact laws” to implement the measure. For example, legislators would have to define which kinds of “government-issued” ID would be acceptable for voting as well as clarify what it means to make a “best effort” to verify a voter’s citizenship status. Prop. 39 would also require the Legislature to establish rules for military and overseas voters that are consistent with federal law.
Allows Citizens to Sue the State or Any County for Not Complying with Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would allow private citizens to sue the state and/or any county for any alleged noncompliance with the initiative. The measure does not specify what kind of evidence would be required to file a lawsuit.
How Would Prop. 39 Affect Californians and the State?
Prop. 39 Would Waste Resources By Addressing a Nonexistent Problem
The voter ID requirements that Prop. 39 would establish provide a “solution” to a nonexistent problem. This measure is based on the false premise that voter fraud — casting a ballot when one is not eligible to vote — is undermining election integrity. However, research shows that voter fraud is exceedingly rare. For example:
Using a comprehensive database tracking election fraud (https://www.brookings.edu/articles/how-widespread-is-election-fraud-in-the-united-states-not-very/) that was created by the right-wing think tank Heritage Foundation, the Brookings Institute found across more than 200 federal elections held in recent decades, the share of fraudulent votes cast were infinitesimally small — ranging from roughly 3 to 15 votes out of 10 million in seven states with close election outcomes. The study concluded that “isolated instances of fraud do not constitute a widespread trend” and that “no election outcome in the US has ever been altered by ballot fraud.”
Summarizing findings across numerous academic studies and investigative reports, the Brennan Center for Justice (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/debunking-voter-fraud-myth) concludes that cases of voter impersonation fraud are extremely rare and do not happen “on a scale even close to that necessary to ‘rig’ an election.” For instance, their seminal report, The Truth About Voter Fraud (https://www.brennancenter.org/media/179/download/Report_Truth-About-Voter-Fraud.pdf?inline=1), concluded that “it is more likely that an individual will be struck by lightning than that [they] will impersonate another voter at the polls.”
Voter fraud among noncitizens is also extremely rare. The Brennan Center (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/noncitizen-voting-vanishingly-rare) synthesized findings from comprehensive studies, state investigations, and nationwide surveys across more than two decades and concluded that “actual incidents of noncitizens voting is not a significant occurrence.” For instance:
One national survey (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/noncitizen-voting-missing-millions) of 44 election administrators representing 42 jurisdictions in 12 states, including officials in eight of the 10 jurisdictions with the largest populations of noncitizens nationally, found that in the 2016 election, officials referred only about 30 incidents of suspected noncitizen voting for further investigation or prosecution — amounting to 0.0001% of votes cast.
The Bipartisan Policy Institute (https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/four-things-to-know-about-noncitizen-voting/) concluded that “there is no evidence that noncitizen voting has ever been significant enough to impact an election’s outcome.” Allegations of noncitizens voting often come out of voter registration audits, but further investigation into these claims often shows that individuals were flagged as noncitizens erroneously.
The libertarian think tank Cato Institute (https://www.cato.org/blog/noncitizens-dont-illegally-vote-detectable-numbers) found that “there is no good evidence that noncitizens voted illegally [in the 2020 election] in large enough numbers to actually shift the outcome of elections or even change the number of electoral votes.”
Additionally, while proponents of Prop. 39 argue that imposing additional ID requirements will strengthen voters’ trust in California’s election process, evidence for this claim is lacking. One study (https://review.law.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2016/08/6_-_Persily_-_Stan._L._Rev.pdf) found that registered voters had roughly equal confidence that votes were counted accurately whether they were in states with strict voter ID laws or states with the minimum ID requirements mandated by federal law.
Subsequent studies by researchers at the University of California Riverside and Western Washington University looking at voter perceptions in 2014 (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1532440015624102?) and following the 2020 US presidential election (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10659129231206179) found that strict voter ID laws and the quality of election administration more generally had little to no effect on voter confidence. This and other research (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10659129241283169) suggests this may be because voters view election laws through a partisan lens and their confidence may be more heavily influenced by partisan rhetoric and whether their preferred candidate wins or loses an election. 13 (javascript:void(0)) See Lonna Rae Atkeson, Eli McKown-Dawson, and Robert M. Stein, “The Costs of Voting and Voter Confidence,” Political Research Quarter

Learn more here (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/). Should California institute new ID requirements for casting a ballot? Below, a former state elections chief says Proposition 39 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-39-voter-id/) will help alleviate doubts in California’s vote. The opposing view: A civic engagement advocate worries the measure will add unnecessary new barriers to a secure and effective system (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/voter-id-barriers-proposition-39/). Guest Commentary written by Bill Jones Bill Jones is a former California secretary of state. During two terms as California’s chief elections officer, my goal in that office was simple: maximum participation and zero tolerance for fraud. Those two things are not in tension. For elections to work, they depend on each other. A voter who doubts the process is a voter who eventually disengages. That’s why I’m supporting Proposition 39 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-39-voter-id/) on this November’s ballot. I hope Californians will join me. Prop. 39 offers three improvements to voting. It requires voters to show government-issued ID to vote in-person or provide the last four digits of a government ID number to vote by mail. It directs the state to issue free ID cards to anyone who needs one, so cost is never a barrier. And it requires election officials to maintain accurate voter rolls, including verifying citizenship — something current law does not meaningfully enforce. It doesn’t disenfranchise eligible voters. Nor does it create a poll tax: The ID is free. It brings California in line with 36 other states that already require some form of voter ID (http://ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/voter-id) and closes a gap that has quietly persisted in our state for years: a voter file that has not been reliably scrubbed of duplicates, deceased voters or people who never should have been added in the first place. This measure arrives at a moment worth paying attention to. It qualified for the ballot this spring (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/04/voter-id-initiative-qualifies/) with signature support from voters of every political stripe. Yet in July, the Attorney General’s office revised the official ballot title (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316615150.html) from a neutral description of what the measure does to language telling voters it “prohibits citizens from voting” unless they show ID. READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) California’s voter ID ballot measure would add unnecessary barriers to a secure system (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/voter-id-barriers-proposition-39/) That’s a striking way to describe a policy that exists in some form in most American states, including states led by both parties. I believe that every eligible voter should vote. That should serve as the basic operating principle of any election system. I’ve seen what happens on both ends of the spectrum. In the late 1990s, I traveled to Mexico with a delegation from the McCain Institute to observe elections after decades of one-party rule had left the system with little credibility. I watched voters present ID and have their fingers inked so they couldn’t vote twice. I can’t say security measures alone broke the one-party grip on Mexico City’s mayoralty that year, but they were part of restoring something the system had lost: public confidence that the count reflected the vote. California doesn’t quite have the same history as Mexico, but we do have a voter file with some inactive records. We automatically mail ballots to people who no longer live there and allow ballot harvesting (https://calmatters.org/politics/2023/10/california-election-voting-republicans/) that simply didn’t exist when I ran elections as secretary of state. None of that means fraud is rampant. It means the system has fewer checks than it used to, at exactly the moment public trust in institutions is at a low ebb. Prop. 39 doesn’t solve every problem in American elections. It does something more modest and more achievable: it makes California’s system harder to doubt. Good election policy isn’t partisan; it’s just good policy. Read more from CalMatters Text Get breaking news on your phone. How a stronger voter ID law can alleviate doubts in California’s election system

By Bill Jones, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

Should California institute new ID requirements for casting a ballot? Below, a former state elections chief says Proposition 39 will help alleviate doubts in California's vote. The opposing view: A civic engagement advocate worries the measure will add unnecessary new barriers to a secure and effective system.

Guest Commentary written by

During two terms as California's chief elections officer, my goal in that office was simple: maximum participation and zero tolerance for fraud. Those two things are not in tension. For elections to work, they depend on each other.

A voter who doubts the process is a voter who eventually disengages. That's why I'm supporting Proposition 39 on this November's ballot. I hope Californians will join me.

Prop. 39 offers three improvements to voting. It requires voters to show government-issued ID to vote in-person or provide the last four digits of a government ID number to vote by mail. It directs the state to issue free ID cards to anyone who needs one, so cost is never a barrier. And it requires election officials to maintain accurate voter rolls, including verifying citizenship — something current law does not meaningfully enforce.

It doesn't disenfranchise eligible voters. Nor does it create a poll tax: The ID is free. It brings California in line with 36 other states that already require some form of voter ID and closes a gap that has quietly persisted in our state for years: a voter file that has not been reliably scrubbed of duplicates, deceased voters or people who never should have been added in the first place.

This measure arrives at a moment worth paying attention to. It qualified for the ballot this spring with signature support from voters of every political stripe. Yet in July, the Attorney General's office revised the official ballot title from a neutral description of what the measure does to language telling voters it "prohibits citizens from voting” unless they show ID.

That's a striking way to describe a policy that exists in some form in most American states, including states led by both parties. I believe that every eligible voter should vote. That should serve as the basic operating principle of any election system.

I've seen what happens on both ends of the spectrum. In the late 1990s, I traveled to Mexico with a delegation from the McCain Institute to observe elections after decades of one-party rule had left the system with little credibility. I watched voters present ID and have their fingers inked so they couldn't vote twice. I can't say security measures alone broke the one-party grip on Mexico City's mayoralty that year, but they were part of restoring something the system had lost: public confidence that the count reflected the vote.

California doesn't quite have the same history as Mexico, but we do have a voter file with some inactive records. We automatically mail ballots to people who no longer live there and allow ballot harvesting that simply didn't exist when I ran elections as secretary of state.

None of that means fraud is rampant. It means the system has fewer checks than it used to, at exactly the moment public trust in institutions is at a low ebb. 

Prop. 39 doesn't solve every problem in American elections. It does something more modest and more achievable: it makes California's system harder to doubt. Good election policy isn't partisan; it's just good policy.

A healthy democracy depends on both public participation and public trust. Without either, the system risks disaffection and loss of legitimacy.
California has made numerous moves in recent years to boost voter participation. From making it easier than ever to vote by mail to overly-liberal ballot harvesting laws, the Golden State has worked to optimize the public participation component of its election administration.
California has also maintained rising levels of public confidence in aspects of its elections. In 2017, just 47% of likely voters and 40% of adults either had “quite a lot of” or a “great deal of” confidence in how California counts votes, according to surveys by the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California. By 2024, those figures rose to 63% and 53%, respectively.
Lurking beneath (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/time-trends-all-adults-1024-corrected.pdf) those 2024 numbers were bigger concerns about election integrity than those figures suggest. The same survey found that 42% of adults and 43% of likely voters said they were “somewhat concerned” or “very concerned” that it’s “too easy for people who are not eligible to vote in California elections.”
Enter Proposition 39.
The proposal seeks to improve public confidence in elections with a simple rule: voters must present a government-issued ID when voting in person or include the last four digits of a government-issued ID that corresponds to identification used at the time of registration on the ballots they intend to mail in. For those who do not have such identification, the measure calls for free identification to be provided for voting.
It also requires election officials to maintain accurate voter registration lists and “use best efforts” to verify citizenship attestations. Finally, it directs regular audits by the State Auditor to ensure compliance with these rules and offer recommendations for how to improve election integrity.
There’s nothing radical about these recommendations. Thirty six states require voters to present some form of identification when voting. Such a requirement is commonplace around the world, including in Canada and Mexico. The logic of identification requirements is quite obvious: it’s simply another check to ensure that people are who they say they are when they vote. In fact, poll workers in California already ask (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/pdfs/trusted-info/trusted-info-voter-id-reg-requirements.pdf) first-time federal election voters who didn’t include an ID number at the time of registration for ID if they show up to the polls.
Opponents of voter identification requirements counter that requiring voters to provide identification at the polls is an unacceptable barrier to democratic participation. We disagree. If people can clear the “barrier” of presenting an ID to buy cigarettes or alcohol or use a credit card or get on an airplane, they can present ID to vote.
Opponents likewise counter that requiring voters to write the last four digits of their ID on their ballots introduces a failure point or privacy risk. We are sympathetic to privacy concerns, though such concerns would be more serious if the rule was to write the total ID number. And the failure point is real — what if voters write the wrong numbers? — but fixable. Ballots can be cured.
Research on the impact of such rules has been mixed over the years, with one review published by the National Bureau of Economic Research in 2019 finding (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5008639) that “strict identification laws are unlikely to have a meaningful impact on turnout or election outcomes.” Echoing this is an analysis published (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5008639) by the journal Research & Politics in December 2024 which found “no compelling evidence that strict voter ID laws consistently suppress or boost voter turnout. Rather, the modest and opposing impacts across contexts appear to net out to minimal aggregate effects on participation, consistent with research showing that electoral reforms often produce small equilibrium effects.”

What could be the most controversial component of the measure is its mandate that election officials use “best efforts” to verify citizenship attestations using “government data.” The measure does not define these terms, thus giving the state and election officials room to figure out how to do that in the most reasonable manner possible. While this editorial board isn’t of the view that noncitizen voting is rampant, it doesn’t seem irrational to occasionally confirm people who attest to their citizenship actually are citizens.
If passed, we expect legal fights over the proposition as a whole and an adjustment period as it’s worked out. Combining the convenience of voting with basic verification isn’t voter suppression — it’s just common-sense governance. Vote Yes on Proposition 39.

Now I have a good steelman. Note the OC Register acknowledges: "Ballots can be cured" — but that's an assumption, not in the text. And "we expect legal fights over the proposition as a whole and an adjustment period."

Key remaining research questions:
1. Does the text provide a cure mechanism? Let me verify — the text says "Election officials shall only count a regular or provisional ballot after verifying the identity of the person voting pursuant to the requirements of this section." No cure provision. Also it's a constitutional amendment, so it would override Elections Code §3019's cure process? Actually a constitutional provision would take precedence over conflicting statutes. But it doesn't explicitly repeal §3019. Hmm — it says ballots shall only be counted after verifying identity. If the ID digits don't match, the ballot can't be counted unless there's a cure. The measure is silent. That's a genuine drafting problem — and importantly, the AG's official title says it "Invalidates mail ballots if envelope does not include last four digits of a government-issued identification number matching the number designated in the voter's registration." So per the AG, the ballot is invalidated — no cure.

2. The re-registration burden: All ~22 million existing registered voters must designate an ID. If they don't, do they get a mail ballot?
