It’s tempting to see state Proposition 39 — the measure authored by local Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio that easily gathered enough signatures to make the November ballot — strictly through the lens of national politics. In requiring voters to show IDs before receiving their ballots, it gives credence to President Donald Trump’s longstanding claim that millions of noncitizens routinely vote in U.S. elections.
But Trump and his allies have never come close to making a case this is a real problem. Voting fraud is rare. Opposing Proposition 39 is a reasonable choice for voters who don’t think the president’s hallucinations should influence election rules.
Nevertheless, it’s also possible to view Proposition 39 and say, “What’s the big deal?” Thirty-six states require (https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_identification_laws_by_state) voters to present identification before voting in person. Just as there is scant evidence of voter fraud, there isn’t much evidence that this requirement is as onerous as voter ID critics insist.
Yet Proposition 39 isn’t just about voter ID. It contains a provision that is deeply problematic: requiring election officials to use their “best efforts” to verify the citizenship status of voters they register, with regular audits to ensure compliance.
But there is no reliable government list of U.S. citizens. Federal databases mostly track the immigration status of people who came from other countries — they don’t include records of the millions of Americans born here. This issue is why employers have long resisted using the federal E-Verify system to check whether workers are legally allowed to work in the U.S.: The data isn’t reliable enough. It’s also why courts have repeatedly blocked similar citizen verification edicts: the legitimate concern that eligible U.S. citizens would be incorrectly identified as ineligible and denied the right to vote.
Election offices already routinely remove voters who have died, moved or otherwise become ineligible. Adding a citizenship verification requirement sounds like a logical next step, but the records needed to do it accurately don’t exist.
Now there is no doubt that some dubious things are being done in state elections. The potential for abuse in “ballot harvesting” — in which a designated person or organization gathers completed mail-in ballots from voters and submits them to election offices, drop boxes or polling locations — is plain. A state law requiring that only individuals known to voters can drop off their ballots should be considered — perhaps as part of an omnibus election reform measure that had as a primary focus speeding up the final reporting of election results by requiring county registrars to begin counting votes the day ballots are mailed, which is already allowed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=15101&lawCode=ELEC) in California.
Such a sensible approach is far preferable to Proposition 39. The U-T Editorial Board urges voters to reject this deeply flawed measure.

Gen. Rob Bonta’s office summarized a strict new voter ID measure on November ballots — ruling that the summary language accurately describes the measure’s effects were it to pass.
Another judge dealt the backers of the measure a second loss by tentatively finding that their description of the measure, submitted for the official state voter’s guide, was misleading. They had claimed that Proposition 39 would make voting easier.
In the first case, Sacramento County Superior Court Judge Jennifer K. Rockwell ruled that the label, title and summary of the certified ballot measure accurately describe Proposition 39 as a measure that “prohibits citizens from voting” — language the measure’s backers specifically objected to — unless they provide a government-issued ID.
Advertisement
According to minutes from a Thursday hearing on the matter, Rockwell concluded that, to the extent the measure’s backers object to that language, they are objecting to “the provisions of the measure itself.”
Rockwell rejected the argument put forth by the measure’s backers that it would not prevent people without ID from voting, only their votes from being counted — a distinction the judge found lacking.
Both parties had asked the court to move quickly ahead of printing deadlines for November ballots.
Advertisement
The attorney general’s office is responsible for preparing titles and summaries for ballot measures, and is not required by law to use the same language as a measure’s proponents when gathering the necessary voter signatures to place the measure on the ballot.
Bonta’s office had argued in court that his office applied the same standard of review to the voter ID measure as every other ballot measure that has come before his office.
Bonta praised Rockwell’s decision on social media (https://x.com/AGRobBonta/status/2085524699954676085) Thursday, writing that it “confirms what we have said from the start: the ballot materials at issue — the ballot title and summary and ballot label — give a true and impartial statement of Proposition 39’s chief purpose and points.”
“My office followed the law and fulfilled its duty to provide California voters with clear, accessible, and accurate information,” he wrote. “We’re pleased that the court agreed with us.”
California Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (R-San Diego), the chief backer of the court challenge and chairman of the group Reform California, responded to the ruling with a video post to social media (https://x.com/carldemaio/status/2085742770434740666), writing that it was “expected” but nonetheless “disappointing.”
DeMaio accused Bonta of trying to “manipulate the vote” with “rigged” language, and Rockwell of being a “liberal judge” who had unsurprisingly decided that Bonta “gets to do corruptly what he wants to do.”
Advertisement
“It’s pissing me off,” DeMaio said in his video post.
DeMaio predicted that Proposition 39 will still pass, but that it will take “all of us spreading the word that the attorney general has tried to manipulate the title on the ballot measure.”
Voter ID requirements are being pushed by Republicans across the country — from President Trump down — as necessary to prevent voter fraud, including by noncitizens, despite elections experts saying that such fraud is exceedingly rare and that there is no evidence that it exists in volumes large enough to swing elections.
Democrats, including in California, have argued that states already have robust measures to ensure that only eligible voters cast ballots, including through existing security measures such as signature verification. They said stricter voter ID requirements would lead to eligible voters without ready access to documents being denied access to voting — including poorer, elderly and rural voters and married women who have changed their names.
A majority of California voters back stricter voter ID requirements, according to recent polls (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-05-09/la-times-igs-poll-on-elections-and-voter-id).
The Trump administration has been pressing for new voter ID requirements nationwide, including in Congress, without success.
Passage of Proposition 39 in liberal California would represent a massive win for the administration and a setback for California’s Democratic leaders. It would require substantial reforms to how the state accepts ballots both in person and through the mail — the latter being the preferred option for the vast majority of voters in recent California elections.

Backers of Proposition 39 also took a hit in a separate court proceeding Thursday, where another judge — siding with top Democratic lawmakers — issued a tentative finding that the measure’s backers were misleading voters by claiming in voter guide language that the measure would make voting easier in the state were it to pass.

The voter guide language will need to change as a result.

Very important findings:

1. A Sacramento Superior Court judge (Chang) found the Yes campaign's claims false and misleading:
   - "makes voting easier" — false
   - "protects privacy" — false; actually makes ID numbers "less private and less secure"
   - "saves millions of dollars" — "objectively untrue"
   - "makes elections more secure" — also challenged

2. The Yes campaign (in an East Bay Times Q&A, Nov 2, 2026) claims Prop 39 "replaces" unreliable signature checks with a 4-digit PIN and "allows a 'curring' process if a voter transposes numbers." BUT: the Mercury News reports "The measure does not repeal signature checks on mail ballots" and "Nothing in Proposition 39 mentions or will affect the signature verification process." So the Yes campaign is now promising a cure process that isn't in the constitutional text. That's a critical gap: since Prop 39 is a constitutional amendment and is "self-executing," and it says officials "shall only count a regular or provisional ballot after verifying the identity of the person voting pursuant to the requirements of this section" — with no cure provision — the promised cure would require the Legislature to pass it, and arguably can't be reconciled with the constitutional text (a statute cannot authorize counting a ballot that the constitution says can only be counted after identity verification).

Actually, hold on. Let's be careful. A cure process could arguably be consistent: the ballot would be counted after the voter cures and identity is verified. But the constitution doesn't provide for notice/cure, and the AG's official title says mail ballots are "invalidated." Under California law, constitutional provisions are supreme over statutes; §3019's cure applies to signature issues, not ID-digit issues. So unless the Legislature passes a new cure process, there is none. And the measure doesn't direct the Legislature to create one. It directs the Legislature to "provide for voting by military and overseas voters" and clarify ID types.

Also critically: the Yes campaign claims it "replaces" signature verification — but the measure doesn't repeal §3019 signature verification. So voters would face BOTH signature matching AND the ID-digit requirement. That means the claim that Prop 39 would eliminate the 100,000 signature-mismatch rejections is false — the signature check remains. That's a major problem: the central "benefit" advertised by the Yes campaign is not in the measure.

Let me verify: Mercury News says "The measure does not specify what qualifies as a unique identifying number and whether its verification would replace the signature verification process." And the Rivas/Limón lawsuit said "Nothing in Proposition 39 mentions or will affect the signature verification process. Proposition 39 adds voter identification requirements, but it does not repeal or change the other procedures that already exist to confirm voter identity under State law." And cityhallpass says "The measure does not repeal signature checks on mail ballots."

So yes: Prop 39 ADDS a requirement on top of existing signature verification. Voters get two chances to have their mail ballot rejected, not one fewer.

3. Fact check on "more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches" in the last election: LA County rejected 7,967 for signature mismatch in Nov 2024 out of 2.76 million. Statewide, in Nov 2024, ~13 million mail ballots. Let me check the statewide number of signature-mismatch rejections. The pro argument says "more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches—and more than 200,000 voters endured hassles just to get their vote to count." Hmm, that seems inflated. Let me verify with data. Actually, Rivas/Limón sought to remove that claim. Let me check what the statewide signature rejection numbers were.

Let me look at the cityhallpass page and search for statewide mail ballot rejection data 2024.

4. Also let me check the "californiatoday.com" analysis, which is detailed and useful.

Let me do these searches.

Proposition 39 : Voter ID for in-person and mail voting
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 39 would require voters to show government-issued ID to vote in person. To vote by mail, voters would have to pick a government ID number for their registration and write its last four digits on each ballot envelope, and ballots would not count if the number does not match. It would also require elections officials to try to verify voters' citizenship and report on it each year, and the state to offer a free voter ID card.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 39 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/).
Results
Polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific on Nov. 3. First results appear here after that.
At a glance
Proposition 39
Voting in person Show government-issued ID every time
Voting by mail Write the last four digits of the ID number you chose at registration; no match, no count
Free voter ID card The state must provide one on request
Cost Tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year, state and local (Legislative Analyst)
LA County voters who used vote centers, Nov. 2024 1,060,354 of 3,793,106 (27.95%)
Money raised, through Nov. 1, 2026 For: $33.0 million (one committee). Against: $33.3 million (three committees, net of transfers)
Largest donor For: Richard Uihlein, $17 million. Against: California Democratic Party, $7.3 million to the three No committees
Latest public poll PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 41% yes, 58% no (likely voters)
Each figure is sourced in the sections below. Money figures are our totals from the committees' state campaign reports, including late contribution reports filed through Nov. 1.
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , What it costs , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 39 mean?
Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
What does a no vote on Proposition 39 mean?
A voter's identity would continue to be established with the voter's signature.
What would Proposition 39 cost?
The Legislative Analyst estimates state and local costs of tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to put the new requirements in place. The amount depends on later decisions, such as how the free ID card is designed and how many people request one.
What it means for the City of LA
The ID rules would apply to every election in California, including City of Los Angeles elections, which the County of Los Angeles now runs for the City. State law today bars cities from requiring voter ID; Proposition 39 would write the requirement into the State Constitution. The Legislative Analyst estimates state and local costs of tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year but gives no figure for the City. The City's proposed 2026-27 budget sets aside $11 million for its general municipal elections.
The details
Official title Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Type Initiative constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by petition signatures
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide
The question on your ballot
Invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Fiscal Impact: Costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. Supporters: The Transparency Foundation; Latino American Political Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; CA Women’s Leadership Assn Opponents: ACLU California Action; Common Cause; League of Women Voters of California
What would change
Today If Proposition 39 passes
Proving who you are when you register Voters give a driver’s license number, state ID number or the last four digits of their Social Security number. Those who do not may be asked for ID the first time they vote (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)) Same, and each voter must also designate one government-issued ID for voting (text, Art. II, Sec. 3.1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Voting in person Voters sign a roster. Officials generally do not verify those signatures before counting (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)) Voters must show government-issued ID every time (text, Sec. 3.1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Voting by mail Voters sign the envelope, and officials check the signature before counting (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)) Voters also write the last four digits of their designated ID number. A ballot counts only after officials verify the number matches (text, Sec. 3.1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)). If a voter uses a different ID’s number than the one designated, the ballot would not count (Attorney General’s summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/title-summary.htm))
Citizenship Voters attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury when they register (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)) The Secretary of State and county officials must use “best efforts” with government data to verify citizenship and report each year the share of each county’s rolls verified (text, Sec. 3.1(a) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Free ID Not applicable The state must give a voter ID card at no charge to any eligible voter who asks (text, Sec. 3.1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Audits Not applicable The State Auditor audits the state’s and each county’s compliance every odd-numbered year (text, Sec. 3.1(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Which elections Not applicable “Any election in the State” (text, Sec. 3.1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
The measure does not say which IDs count. It defines government-issued ID only as documentation “that allows conclusive verification of the voter’s identity” (text, Sec. 3.1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)). The Legislative Analyst says the Legislature would have to pass laws to settle which forms of ID are accepted and what counts as “best efforts” on citizenship (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)). The measure does not repeal signature checks on mail ballots.
What it would mean for City of Los Angeles elections
It would cover City elections. The ID rule applies to “any election in the State” (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)), and the Legislative Analyst says each ballot cast “in any election in California” would need the added ID information (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)).
The County runs them. City elections for Mayor, Council, other City offices and City measures are held in even-numbered years. Since 2020 the County of Los Angeles has run most of the work of those elections (City Clerk (https://clerk.lacity.gov/elections)).
Today a city cannot require ID. A 2024 state law bars any city, including a charter city, from requiring ID to vote “unless required by state or federal law” (Elections Code Sec. 10005, SB 1174 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB1174)). Courts blocked Huntington Beach’s voter-approved voter ID charter amendment, and in January 2026 the State Supreme Court declined to review the appeals court ruling (Orange County Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/01/29/california-supreme-court-wont-review-huntington-beachs-voter-id-law-leaving-appeals-court-decision-against-the-city/)). Proposition 39 would put the requirement in the State Constitution.
How Angelenos vote now. In the November 2024 election, 2,732,752 of the 3,793,106 Los Angeles County ballots (72.05%) were cast by mail and 1,060,354 (27.95%) at vote centers (LA County Registrar (https://results.lavote.gov/text-results/4324)). Under Prop. 39, the first group would add ID digits to the envelope and the second would show ID.
Rejected mail ballots in LA County. In November 2024 the County rejected 21,356 of 2,764,734 returned mail ballots (0.77%), including 7,967 for signatures that did not match and 3,272 with no signature (Secretary of State (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/vbm-rejection-reason/2024/november-general-2024.pdf)). In the June 2026 primary it rejected 24,806 (1.34%), including 7,190 for mismatched signatures (Secretary of State (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/vbm-rejection-reason/2026/june-primary-2026.pdf)).
Cost. The Legislative Analyst estimates state and local costs of tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year and gives no figure for any one city or county (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)). The City’s proposed 2026-27 budget holds $11 million for general municipal election expenses, up from $10 million in 2025-26 (CAO, Unappropriated Balance (https://cao.lacity.gov/content/budget/26-27/2026-27ProposedBudget.pdf#page=255)).
Neighborhood Council elections. The City Clerk runs Neighborhood Council elections in odd-numbered years (City Clerk (https://clerk.lacity.gov/elections)). Voters in them need not be U.S. citizens, and the voting age is 16 (EmpowerLA (https://neighborhoodempowerment.lacity.gov/elections/)). Neither the measure nor the Legislative Analyst says whether these elections would count as an “election in the State” for the ID rule.
Timing. The Nov. 3, 2026 election, with the City’s Mayor race (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/races/mayor) and eight City measures (City Clerk list (https://cityclerk.lacity.org/onlinedocs/2026/26-1100-S8_misc_08-03-26.pdf)), runs under current rules, since an approved amendment takes effect only after the vote is certified (Cal. Const., Art. XVIII, Sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)). Under the City’s even-year schedule, the next regular City election would be in 2028 (City Clerk (https://clerk.lacity.gov/elections)).
How it got on the ballot
Proposition 39 is a citizen initiative, placed on the ballot by voter petitions.
Sept. 19, 2025: The Attorney General issued the petition’s title and summary. The proponents are Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, Sen. Tony Strickland and Donald J. DiCostanzo (Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)). LAist describes DeMaio and Strickland as the two Republican legislators behind it (LAist (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-proposition-39)).
Oct. 21, 2025: The campaign reported gathering 25% of the signatures needed (Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
March 2026: Petitions were filed with the counties. They held 1,367,961 raw signatures, 264,563 of them from Los Angeles County (Secretary of State random sample count (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/1984-finalrandomsample-04-24-26.pdf)). That is about 19% from Los Angeles County (our calculation).
April 24, 2026: The random sample projected 1,027,018 valid signatures, more than 110% of the 874,641 needed, and the measure became eligible (Secretary of State random sample count (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/1984-finalrandomsample-04-24-26.pdf)).
Title change (July-Aug. 2026): Voters had signed the petition under the title “Establishes Additional Voter Identification and Citizenship Verification Requirements” (Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)). The ballot title is “Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification” (guide (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/title-summary.htm)). The Yes campaign sued over the new title. On Aug. 6, Sacramento Superior Court Judge Jennifer K. Rockwell ruled that the title, summary and label “accurately describe the effect of the measure.” In a separate suit by Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas and Senate President pro Tem Monique Limón, Judge Shelleyanne Chang tentatively found misleading the Yes argument’s claim that the measure would make voting easier (LA Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-08-07/judge-rejects-challenge-to-california-attorney-generals-description-of-voter-id-measure); Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/08/03/california-voter-id-prop-39-both-sides-sue/)).
Vote needed. As a constitutional amendment, it passes with a majority of votes cast statewide (Cal. Const., Art. XVIII, Sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the opinions of their authors and have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument for, signed by the Democratic, Republican and Independent coalition chairs of Californians for Voter ID, Margit Whitlock, Tafa Jefferson and Joe Green (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
Trust: voter ID is “a common-sense reform to increase trust and participation.”
Access: mail ballots and extended hours stay, and every voter can get a free ID.
Signatures: “In the last election, more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches.”
Turnout: states with voter ID and free IDs have “seen an increase in voting.”
Audits: an independent audit every two years and citizenship checks of the rolls.
The opponents’ rebuttal, signed by U.S. Sen. Alex Padilla, the California Nurses Association and the California School Employees Association, says the measure is funded by “MAGA rightwing billionaires,” that Texas threw out “12 times more mail ballots than California” under similar rules, and that the Legislative Analyst found it could cost “hundreds of millions each year” (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument against, signed by David Trujillo of ACLU California Action, Darius Kemp of Common Cause and Lorrel Plimier of the League of Women Voters of California (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
Motive: it ties the measure to President Trump’s claims about elections.
Cost: “hundreds of millions of dollars.”
Privacy: writing ID digits on the envelope exposes voters to identity theft.
Rejected ballots: one wrong digit, an outdated address or a changed name could cause a valid ballot to be rejected, and voters who do not designate an ID “may not get a mail ballot at all.”
Hidden costs: a “free” ID still costs travel, time off and documents.
The supporters’ rebuttal, signed by the Transparency Foundation, the California Women’s Leadership Association and the Latino American Political Association, says the measure “is not about Donald Trump or Gavin Newsom” and that “states with voter ID laws have not seen decreases in voter participation” (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Outside the guide.
California Republican Party Chair Corrin Rankin: “ID is required for so many things that we do in life” (ABC7 (https://abc7.com/post/what-know-proposition-39-californias-voter-id-measure/19872464/)).
Democratic candidate for governor Xavier Becerra said a voter who registered under a maiden name and votes under a married name could have the vote blocked (ABC7 (https://abc7.com/post/what-know-proposition-39-californias-voter-id-measure/19872464/)).
DeMaio called it a “superior model” to the federal SAVE America Act because it keeps mail voting (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/08/03/california-voter-id-prop-39-both-sides-sue/)).
LA County Supervisor Holly Mitchell: “LA County’s elections are already secure, and Prop 39 does nothing to make them safer” (City News Service via Westside Current (https://www.westsidecurrent.com/county_news/county-leaders-enter-the-fight-over-proposed-voter-id-laws/article_de479320-c977-4c0a-8545-822fee0f22b6.html)).
County registrars interviewed by ABC7 said checking partial ID numbers could take longer than signature checks (ABC7 (https://abc7.com/post/what-know-proposition-39-californias-voter-id-measure/19872464/)).
Checking the main factual claims against official records.
Claim Who makes it What official records show
More than 100,000 ballots were rejected for signature mismatches “in the last election” Yes campaign The argument does not name the election. Statewide, 71,387 mail ballots were rejected for non-matching signatures in November 2024 and 43,976 in the June 2026 primary (Secretary of State, Nov. 2024 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/vbm-rejection-reason/2024/november-general-2024.pdf); June 2026 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/vbm-rejection-reason/2026/june-primary-2026.pdf)). We did not find a statewide election with more than 100,000
Voter ID would replace slow signature checks Yes campaign (implied) The measure adds ID digits and does not repeal signature checks (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)). Rivas and Limón made the same point in court (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/08/03/california-voter-id-prop-39-both-sides-sue/))
An independent audi

# California elections officials rejected 122,000 ballots in 2024 election. Here’s why
SACRAMENTO, Calif.
— Elections officials around California threw out 122,480 vote-by-mail ballots cast during the November general election, or 0.9% of all mail-in ballots, according to data from the Secretary of State’s office.
The vast majority of those were tossed because they arrived late, had mismatched voter signatures or no signature at all.
...
An analysis of mail ballot rejections during the 2024 election by USC’s Center for Inclusive Democracy found that 59% had a nonmatching voter signature, 27% were mailed or arrived after the deadline, and 11% had no signature.
The other 3% were thrown out for other unspecified reasons.

Wheres My Ballot?
program stating, “your ballot for the March Election has been received, but we are having trouble processing it.”
2. You have a right to access a form on your county election ofcial’s website to provide your signature and confrm that you voted your ballot.
Fill out the form and follow the instructions on how to return the completed form.
...
Failure to follow instructions may result in your ballot not being counted.
...
3. You have the right to fx your missing or mismatched signature before the deadline.
The deadline is 5 p.m. two days prior to the day your county certifes the election.
...

# Vote-By-Mail Ballot Rejection Reason Reports - Legislative and Congressional Vacancy Elections, 2024
In accordance with Elections Code section 15377, elections officials must provide to the Secretary of State the number of vote-by-mail ballots rejected, categorized according to the reason for the rejection, within 31 days of every election.
Upon receipt of this information, for every election starting with the June 7, 2022, Primary Election, the Secretary of State will publish Vote-by-Mail Ballot Rejection Reason Reports.
Rejection reason data is provided by county elections officials to the Secretary of State through the VoteCal system.

5. General Election: Ballot Identification Envelopes: Noncomparable Signatures and Unsigned Envelopes
https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ccrov/2024/september/24210rd.pdf
County elections officials shall not reject a vote-by-mail ballot or a provisional ballot for the reason of noncomparable signatures if one of the following occurs:
1) The voter completes and submits a Signature Verification Statement (or the combined statement) to a polling location within the county or a ballot drop-off box, before the close of the polls on Election Day, or
2) The voter delivers, in person, by mail, by fax, by email, or by other means, a 
Signature Verification Statement (or the combined statement) signed by the voter and no later than 5 p.m. two days prior to the certification of the election*, and the county elections official receives the voter’s completed Signature
Verification Statement, 
and 
the voter’s signature on the Signature Verification Statement (or the combined statement) compares with the signature(s) in the voter’s registration record.
...
If the signature on the Signature Verification Statement (or the combined statement) does not compare, the ballot identification envelope shall not be opened, the ballot shall not be counted, and the elections official shall write the cause of the rejection on the face of the identification envelope.
...
• An exact match is not required for an elections official to determine that a voter’s signature is valid.
The fact that signatures share similar characteristics is sufficient to determine that a signature is valid.
• The elections official shall consider explanations for discrepancies between signatures

Excellent — the fact-check is decisive on one key claim:

The Yes campaign's central factual claim in the official voter guide — "In the last election, more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches" — is FALSE per Secretary of State data: statewide, 71,387 mail ballots were rejected for non-matching signatures in November 2024 (and 43,976 in June 2026 primary). Total rejections of all kinds in Nov 2024 were 122,480 (0.9%), and signature mismatch was 59% of those. So "more than 100,000 rejected due to signature mismatches" overstates the actual number by ~40%.

Also key: the Yes campaign claims Prop 39 would "replace unreliable signature checks" — but the measure does NOT repeal signature verification. So it's additive, not a replacement. This is the single biggest substantive misrepresentation: the main benefit advertised is not in the text.

And the Yes campaign's promised "cure process" for transposed digits is not in the text either (the East Bay Times Q&A on Nov 2, 2026 claims it "allows a 'curring' process" — but the constitutional text has no cure provision, and the AG's official title says such ballots are "invalidated").

Let me also read the rest of the cityhallpass page for the remaining fact-check rows and "If it passes" section. And let me check the Mercury News endorsement and the LAist voter guide for any additional analysis. Also let me check the "californiatoday.com" analysis about the absence of a cure provision — that seemed authoritative.

Let me also verify one more thing: does the measure risk disenfranchising voters who don't designate an ID? And what about San Francisco/Oakland noncitizen school board voting — Prop 39's citizenship verification could conflict with those local programs. The measure requires "best efforts to verify citizenship attestations" — and SF/Oakland allow noncitizen parents to vote in school board elections. Interesting tension.

Also: LA Neighborhood Council elections where non-citizens and 16-year-olds can vote — "Neither the measure nor the Legislative Analyst says whether these elections would count as an 'election in the State.'"

Let me fetch the rest of cityhallpass and the californiatoday analysis.

t every two years Yes campaign The State Auditor must audit compliance every odd-numbered year (text, Sec. 3.1(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Costs “hundreds of millions” a year No campaign The Legislative Analyst’s range is tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year, under 0.25% of the state General Fund (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm))
Voters who do not designate an ID “may not get a mail ballot” No campaign The Attorney General’s summary says the measure “prohibits voting by mail unless voter designates a government-issued identification number” (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/title-summary.htm))
Funded by out-of-state billionaires No campaign Richard Uihlein, whose filings give a Wisconsin address, gave $17 million, 51.6% of the Yes committee’s money. Donors outside California gave 80.3% (Cal-Access (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1479607))
Who supports and opposes it
Supporters
Californians for Voter ID and Reform California, led by Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (Cal-Access (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1479607); LA Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-08-07/judge-rejects-challenge-to-california-attorney-generals-description-of-voter-id-measure)).
The Transparency Foundation, Latino American Political Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and California Women’s Leadership Association (ballot label (https://content.lavote.gov/docs/rrcc/documents/final-measures-appearing-on-the-ballot-8-20-2026-v-12.pdf); argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
California Republican Party, Republican candidate for governor Steve Hilton, Rep. Ken Calvert and Sen. Tony Strickland (LAist (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-proposition-39)).
Opponents
ACLU California Action, Common Cause and the League of Women Voters of California (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
U.S. Sen. Alex Padilla, the California Nurses Association and the California School Employees Association (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
California Democratic Party, the California Labor Federation and the UCLA Voting Rights Project (LAist (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-proposition-39)).
Xavier Becerra and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas, honorary co-chairs of one No committee (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/08/03/california-voter-id-prop-39-both-sides-sue/)).
Los Angeles County Supervisors Hilda Solis, Holly Mitchell, Lindsey Horvath and Janice Hahn (City News Service via Westside Current (https://www.westsidecurrent.com/county_news/county-leaders-enter-the-fight-over-proposed-voter-id-laws/article_de479320-c977-4c0a-8545-822fee0f22b6.html)).
Editorial boards. The Sacramento Bee recommends no (Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317017898.html); MSN copy (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/should-california-require-voter-and-citizenship-id-our-prop-39-endorsement-opinion/ar-AA2cQyjI)). The Mercury News and East Bay Times editorial boards also recommend no: “Reject Prop. 39” (Mercury News, Oct. 15, 2026 (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/15/endorsement-reject-proposition-39-voter-id-fraud-ballot-measure/)). The San Diego Union-Tribune editorial board “urges voters to reject this deeply flawed measure.” It objected most to the provision requiring officials to use “best efforts” to verify citizenship, writing that “the records needed to do it accurately don’t exist” (San Diego Union-Tribune, Oct. 2, 2026 (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/02/endorsement-vote-no-on-prop-39-and-its-unworkable-voter-registration-rule/)). The San Francisco Chronicle editorial board “recommends a no vote” and wrote that the measure “is almost certain to disenfranchise eligible voters” (San Francisco Chronicle, Oct. 12, 2026 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-proposition-39-voter-fraud-california-22463918.php)). The Daily News editorial board recommends yes: “Vote Yes on Proposition 39” (Daily News, Oct. 15, 2026 (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/10/15/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-39/)). We found no LA Times editorial board position as of Sept. 30, 2026. The LA Times ran an op-ed in favor by an outside contributor (LA Times (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2026-09-24/proposition-39-california-voter-id-law)).
We found no position from Mayor Karen Bass or the City Council as of Sept. 30, 2026.
Money for and against
For Prop. 39 Against Prop. 39
Committees Californians for Voter ID, Yes on 39 No on 39 - Block Election Rigging; No on Prop 39 - Californians for Voting Rights; United Against Prop. 39 - Stop the Rig
Raised, through Oct. 17, 2026 $32,752,567.94 $31,609,593.28
Late contributions, Oct. 18 to Nov. 1 $215,981.60 $1,692,261.87
Total reported $32,968,549.54 $33,301,855.15
Cash on hand, Oct. 17 $780,173.33 $7,452,039.89
Source: each committee’s campaign statements (Form 460), the latest covering Sept. 20 to Oct. 17 (Yes on 39 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3216069&amendid=0); Block Election Rigging (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3215267&amendid=0); Californians for Voting Rights (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3215625&amendid=0); Stop the Rig (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3215264&amendid=0)), and late contribution reports (Form 497) filed through Nov. 1, in the Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip) dated Nov. 2, 2026, analyzed by CityHallPass. Committee pages: Yes on 39 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1479607), Block Election Rigging (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1493991), Californians for Voting Rights (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1489007), Stop the Rig (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1495206). The “against” totals subtract the money the No committees passed to each other: $5,669,472 from Block Election Rigging to Stop the Rig ($2.15 million of it on late reports) and a $500,000 late gift from Californians for Voting Rights to Stop the Rig. The Yes figure counts from Jan. 1, 2025; counting only 2026, the Yes committee raised $23,942,372.48 through Oct. 17. A fourth listed No committee, VoteRiders, reported no contributions through Oct. 17 (VoteRiders statement (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3214981&amendid=0); Secretary of State totals (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-39-establishes-additional-voter-identification-and-citizenship-verification-requirements-initiative-constitutional-a)). The LA Times reported $39.3 million raised by opponents and $15.6 million by supporters (LA Times, Sept. 28, 2026 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-28/200-million-plus-raised-billionaire-tax-measure-november-ballot)). We could not match the opponents’ figure to the committee filings.
Who is giving
Method: every itemized contribution on the committees’ statements from Jan. 1, 2025 through Oct. 17, 2026, plus late contribution reports after that date filed through Nov. 1, from the Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip). Different spellings of one donor are merged. Shares are ours.
For. The Yes committee reported 473 donors. Richard Uihlein, whose employer is listed as Uline, gave $17 million in three gifts from December 2025 to September 2026, 51.6% of the total. Joseph Gebbia, whose employer is listed as Samara, gave $8 million on Oct. 6, 24.3%. Reform California, DeMaio’s ballot measure committee, gave $3.16 million, nearly all as in-kind signature gathering. Other large donors were Nicole Shanahan ($370,000), Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss ($250,000 each) and Sequoia Capital’s Douglas Leone ($250,000). Donors outside California gave $26.5 million (80.3%). A $300,000 gift from Perfect One Capital was later refunded (Cal-Access (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1479607)). Reform California itself raised $6.98 million from Jan. 2025 to Oct. 17, 2026, from more than 14,000 itemized donors plus $1.46 million in gifts under $100 (Cal-Access (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1268914); Sept. 20 to Oct. 17 statement (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3216024&amendid=0)).
Against. The largest No committee, Block Election Rigging, reported 59 donors. The largest were the California Democratic Party ($4.53 million), the Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria ($2 million), the SEIU California State Council ($1.07 million), and the California Teachers Association’s Issues PAC, SEIU Local 2015’s Dignity CA committee and Reed Hastings ($1 million each). Eight union committees, including a second California Teachers Association committee, gave $500,000 each (Cal-Access (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1493991)). The ACLU-sponsored committee’s largest donors were M. Quinn Delaney and Patty Quillin, $1.5 million each (Cal-Access (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1489007)).
How the money was spent. Through Oct. 17, the Yes committee paid Flexpoint Media $14.77 million, 51.2% of its cash payments, and GOCO Partners $7.07 million for petitions, 24.5% (Cal-Access (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1479607); Sept. 20 to Oct. 17 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3216069&amendid=0)). On Oct. 13 it paid Block Election Rigging $85,000, which its statement describes as “Attorney Fees per Settlement” (Sept. 20 to Oct. 17 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3216069&amendid=0)). Block Election Rigging paid AL Media $9.89 million for television and online ads (Cal-Access (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1493991); Sept. 20 to Oct. 17 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3215267&amendid=0)).
Outside spending
New since Oct. 25 in the Cal-Access raw data dated Nov. 2 (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip): the Republican Party of San Diego County reported $40,378.81 for literature on Oct. 26 and $4,874.54 for texts on Oct. 28, and Reform California reported $30,000 in digital ads on Oct. 31, all supporting the measure (Form 496). These are not in the figures below.
Reform California filed 24-hour independent expenditure reports of $1,611,559.17 supporting the measure through Oct. 25. The Republican Party of San Diego County reported $100,062.47 in support. Republican legislators’ ballot measure committees, including those of Assemblymember David Tangipa ($72,743.84) and Sen. Tony Strickland ($20,000), reported smaller amounts. Against the measure, Faith Votes, sponsored by PICO California Action Fund, reported $88,183.33 and the Committee to Save Our Neighborhoods, sponsored by the Alliance of Californians for Community Empowerment, $56,500. Seven other groups reported $2,793.31 to $14,850 each in opposition (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
Independent analysis
Legislative Analyst. Costs of tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year for the state and counties, under 0.25% of the General Fund. Some savings could come from fewer people on the rolls, but “likely would not exceed the costs” (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)).
Scale of voting by mail. About 13 million of the roughly 16 million Californians who voted in November 2024 used mail ballots (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)). Statewide, 122,439 returned mail ballots (0.92%) were rejected that election, and 148,427 (1.73%) in the June 2026 primary, most of them for arriving late (Secretary of State, Nov. 2024 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/vbm-rejection-reason/2024/november-general-2024.pdf); June 2026 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/vbm-rejection-reason/2026/june-primary-2026.pdf)). The Associated Press reported that the June rise was driven by late postmarks (AP via LAist (https://laist.com/brief/news/politics/nearly-150-000-mail-ballots-rejected-california-primary)).
Noncitizen voting. LAist reports that efforts to find and prosecute noncitizen voters “have thus far turned up few culprits” (LAist (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-proposition-39)).
We found no City or County estimate of what the measure would cost Los Angeles.
If it passes
Effective date. A constitutional amendment takes effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote (Cal. Const., Art. XVIII, Sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)). The measure says it is “self-executing” (text, Sec. 3.1(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)).
Laws to follow. The Legislature must “promptly enact laws” to carry it out, including rules for military and overseas voters. The Legislative Analyst says it would have to define which IDs count (text, Sec. 3.1(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2); analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)).
Every voter re-designates. New and existing voters would have to choose an ID in their registration to vote by mail (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)).
Enforcement. Any citizen may sue over the state’s or a county’s compliance (text, Sec. 3.1(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)). The text requires the State Auditor to audit compliance “during every odd-numbered year” (text, Sec. 3.1(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)).
Legal challenges. We found no filed challenge to the measure’s substance as of Sept. 30, 2026.
Key moments
Huntington Beach ruling stands (Jan. 28, 2026). The State Supreme Court declined to review the ruling against that city’s voter ID law. Sen. Tony Strickland, a Prop. 39 proponent, had co-signed the ballot argument for the city’s measure as a councilmember (Orange County Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/01/29/california-supreme-court-wont-review-huntington-beachs-voter-id-law-leaving-appeals-court-decision-against-the-city/); Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
Ballot title fight (July-Aug. 2026). The Attorney General changed the title for the ballot. The Yes campaign sued and lost on Aug. 6. DeMaio called the ruling “expected” but “disappointing”; Attorney General Rob Bonta said the court confirmed the ballot materials were accurate and impartial (LA Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-08-07/judge-rejects-challenge-to-california-attorney-generals-description-of-voter-id-measure); Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/08/03/california-voter-id-prop-39-both-sides-sue/)).
LA County supervisors oppose (Sept. 21, 2026). Four of the five supervisors endorsed the No campaign (City News Service via Westside Current (https://www.westsidecurrent.com/county_news/county-leaders-enter-the-fight-over-proposed-voter-id-laws/article_de479320-c977-4c0a-8545-822fee0f22b6.html)).
We found no debate between the campaigns in news coverage as of Sept. 30, 2026.

Proposition 39 would make California the latest state to require ID to vote, replacing signature checks on 13 million mail ballots with a four-digit ID match. Here is how voting works today, exactly what the measure changes, what it would cost, and who is paying for each side.
by
Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/mac/)
Updated
October 08, 2026

California voter ID rules would change for every in-person and mail voter under Proposition 39 on the November 3, 2026 ballot.
Proposition 39 asks California voters to write a voter identification requirement into the state Constitution. If it passes, every voter would present government-issued identification to vote in person, and every mail voter, which in November 2024 meant about 13 million of the 16 million who voted, would write the last four digits of a designated ID number on the ballot envelope, where today they sign their name. The measure, placed on the ballot (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/) by petition and sponsored by Reform California's Carl DeMaio, is one of the 14 statewide propositions in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/), and it is the one whose polling the campaigns dispute most.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California’s November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure’s rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) The measure is short, about 400 words of operative text, and much of the argument around it concerns what those words leave out. This explainer sets out how voting in California works now, what Prop 39's text actually requires, what the Legislative Analyst says it would cost, how two Sacramento judges ruled on the campaigns' language in August, and who is funding each side.
Proposition 39 is changing the verification step for in-person and mail voting in California from a signature to a government-issued identification number, as the measure's text and the Elections Code show in October 2026.
Proposition 39 adds one section to the Constitution with three requirements
The measure's text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf) adds Section 3.1 to Article II of the California Constitution. Its findings say the purpose is "to deter and detect voter fraud by maintaining accurate voter registration records and confirming eligibility to vote" and "to minimize the risk of voter impersonation by requiring proof of identity to vote." The operative provisions are three.
First, citizenship verification: the Secretary of State and county elections officials "shall use best efforts to verify citizenship attestations using government data, and shall annually report what percentage of each county's voter rolls have been citizenship-verified."
Second, identification at the ballot: "Each time a voter casts a ballot in person in any election in the State, the voter shall present government-issued identification, or if voting by mail, the voter shall provide the last four digits of a unique identifying number from government-issued identification that matches the one designated by the voter for their voter registration." The type of ID each voter designates must be recorded in their registration and printed on their mail-ballot envelope. Officials "shall only count a regular or provisional ballot after verifying the identity of the person voting pursuant to the requirements of this section." The measure's only definition of acceptable ID is that it "means documentation that allows conclusive verification of the voter's identity," and it requires the state to provide "at no charge, a voter ID card" to any eligible voter who asks.
Third, enforcement: the section is "self-executing," the Legislature "shall also promptly enact laws to implement" it, citizens may seek judicial review of any county's compliance, and in every odd-numbered year the State Auditor must audit the state and every county and report publicly.
The Attorney General's summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/title-summary.htm) draws out a consequence the text implies but does not spell out: the measure "invalidates mail ballots if envelope does not include last four digits of a government-issued identification number matching the number designated in the voter's registration (e.g., if voter designates Social Security number for registration, but provides driver's license number on envelope, their ballot would not count)." Nothing in the measure describes what happens next. There is no notice-and-cure provision of the kind that exists today for signature mismatches, and no list of which documents qualify. The LAO's analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm) says the Legislature "would need to clarify several details that are not defined in the proposition, like which forms of identification could be used and what steps would be considered best efforts to verify the citizenship status of registered voters."
Voting in California today runs on signatures, not identification
The Secretary of State's own guidance (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voting-resources/voting-california/what-bring) to voters begins: "In most cases, a California voter is not required to show identification to a polling place worker before casting a ballot." Under Elections Code section 14216 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=14216), an in-person voter states their name and address, the poll worker finds them in the roster, and the voter signs. One more important angle: does Prop 39 conflict with federal law (HAVA) for mail voters? HAVA §301(b) requires first-time mail registrants to provide ID, but states can be stricter. However, requiring ID numbers on envelopes for ALL mail voters could conflict with... actually no federal preemption issue there. But there's a potential issue with UOCAVA/military overseas voters — the text explicitly directs the Legislature to handle that "consistent with federal law."

Would Prop 39 speed up or slow down California’s vote-counting?
By Sara DiNatale (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/sara-dinatale/) , Staff Writer Oct 11, 2026
Marion Gautier helps organize and count absentee and mail-in ballots at the San Francisco Department of Elections at City Hall on Nov. 6, 2019.
Gabrielle Lurie/S.F. Chronicle
Most of the conservatives who critique California’s election system have two separate complaints: They believe California’s vote-counting process is riddled with fraud, and they think the state takes far too long to count its votes. (Many say that the latter is evidence of the former.)
Backers of Proposition 39, a measure to implement voter ID requirements, say their plan will solve both issues. Experts, however, say the measure’s requirements would slow down, not speed up, vote-counting.
Chronicle endorsements: Editorial Board’s recommendations for 2026 election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 39 would require voters to show government-issued identification each time they cast a ballot in person. People who vote by mail would have to register a PIN that’s either the last four digits of their Social Security number or their driver’s license number. They could also request a free “voter ID” with a number on it. The number would need to be handwritten on the ballot envelope. Election offices would then have to check and verify the number. Critics say that means essentially 26 million people would have to reregister to vote across California.
The proposition’s cocreator, Assembly Member Carl DeMaio, R-San Diego, has cast Prop 39 as a simple and necessary change to fortify voters’ trust in state elections. During a May episode of his podcast, DeMaio said the measure’s requirement of a four-digit PIN would replace the signature verification process for the more than 80% of voters using mail-in ballots. He said that if Prop 39 becomes law, mail-in ballots would be processed “literally within 48 hours of them coming back.”
Meredith Shields, the press secretary for the Yes on 39 campaign, reiterated those claims in a statement on Friday, saying “providing a four-digit PIN when voting by mail, election officials will not have to match electronic signatures.”
But the measure does not contain any language about the PIN numbers usurping signature verification, which is codified in state law. That means the new handwritten PINs would be required and verified in addition to signatures, not in lieu of them, voting experts said.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The state’s official voter guide lays out what a yes vote means: “Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote” — language that suggests the PIN is an extra layer of verification, not a replacement.
“Voters can read the language of Prop 39 for themselves,” said Brittany Stonesifer, an attorney and voting rights advocate with nonprofit California Common Cause. “It would add additional requirements for mail ballots. It says nothing about removing the existing signature verification process.”
DeMaio suggested during his podcast that there would be a “scanning” system for the PIN numbers, but that would require infrastructure and technology that election offices don’t yet have.
“The notion that this will speed up the process is asinine,” said Stephen Richer, a Republican former recorder of Maricopa County, Ariz. “I don’t know how having an additional requirement could possibly make the process go faster.”
Richer said he broadly supports ID checks at polling places to verify that the person trying to vote matches the person recorded in the voter rolls. California doesn’t do that. Voters must present a government ID when they register to vote, but when voting in person they only must provide poll workers with their name and address, and sign a voter roster.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
“It would absolutely result in valid mail ballots being rejected, potentially at a high level, with no evidence that it would increase security,” Stonesifer said of the four-digit PIN numbers.
Assembly Member Gail Pellerin, D-Santa Cruz, who is the head of the Assembly Elections Committee and a former elections official, agrees. She told the Los Angeles Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/newsletter/2026-09-28/skelton-monday-politics-newsletter-voter-id) that under Prop 39, not only would some voters’ ballots be rejected by mistake but the measure would “absolutely” slow down counting.
Richer, Stonesifer, Pellerin and other voting experts largely agree signature verification is a secure and efficient way to vet mail-in ballots. Some election offices use software to quickly confirm a signature match and kick any questionable ones to workers who can pull up someone’s state signature history to see how it may have changed over time.
If the signature still looks odd, they notify the voter it needs to be fixed. California has a long window allowing ballot curing, which is a common criticism of the state’s lagging vote-tallying process. But legislation just signed into law by Gov. Gavin Newsom requires all counties to allow digital signature curing in order to speed the process.
Shields, the Prop 39 campaign spokesperson, said the measure would not only speed the process, but would conserve resources.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
“When Prop 39 passes, IDs will be free of charge and the verification and counting of ballots will be faster, more accurate, and will save election officials valuable time and resources,” she said.
The state’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, however, estimates the measure would cost the state and local governments tens of millions to hundreds of millions of dollars. Darius Kemp, the director of Common Cause California, said the measure would also take resources away from counties and clerks, impeding them from counting more quickly.
Pamela Smith, president of Verified Voting, a nonprofit focused on election security, said that if someone was so determined to cheat that they would spoof a signature, there’s no reason to believe they wouldn’t also pilfer a PIN. She, too, was wary that the measure would speed up the count.
“The costs to taxpayers associated with implementation are significant, which might not matter if this were a game changer for efficiency or security, but it is neither,” Smith said.
Prop 39 does not include a curing process for PIN codes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
“My mother has very interesting handwriting,” Rep. Lateefah Simon, D-Oakland, said during a Friday rally against Prop 39. “If, in fact, the registrar of voters cannot read her handwriting or her Social Security number ... what will happen to her ballot? It will be discarded.”
State Sen. Jesse Arreguín, D-Berkeley, also argued the measure will impede in-person voting.
“Repetitive ID checks under Prop 39 are not only unnecessary, they will slow our checking and create longer lines and delays for people to vote and make it harder for them to participate in their right to vote,” Arreguín said during the Friday rally in Oakland.
Stonesifer said funding more staffers in election offices — rather than implementing a new system to scan four-digit codes — would be a better way to speed up the counting process.
DeMaio and his critics do agree on one thing: They’re all encouraging voters to return their ballots early. One of the biggest factors that slows California’s tabulation is the surge of vote-by-mail ballots returned on Election Day.

Sara DiNatale covers politics and the impacts of the Trump administration’s policies on the Bay Area and California. She joined the Chronicle in 2025, after a decade reporting across the southern United States for the San Antonio Express-News, the Tampa Bay Times and Mississippi Today.

It’s impossible not to view Proposition 39 — the measure authored by Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio and backed by out-of-state, right-wing billionaires (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-voter-id-proposition-39/) — strictly through the lens of national politics.
In requiring voters to show IDs before receiving their ballots (among other restrictive voting rules and audits), it gives credence to President Donald Trump’s longstanding and repeatedly debunked claims that millions of noncitizens routinely vote in U.S. elections.
Related Articles
Endorsement: Break the 49ers’ grip over Santa Clara. Elect these three candidates. (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/31/endorsement-break-the-49ers-grip-over-santa-clara-make-kertes-mayor-elect-inciarte-and-crutchlow-to-council/)
Endorsement: These three City Council candidates are San Jose’s best choices (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-peter-ortiz-bien-doan-and-genny-altwer-to-san-jose-city-council/)
Endorsement: Elect Michael Melillo to San Jose Unified School District Board of Education (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-michael-melillo-to-san-jose-unified-school-district-board-of-education/)
Endorsement: Reject San Mateo Community College District’s $848 million Measure V (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-reject-san-mateo-community-college-districts-848-million-measure-v/)
Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
This initiative is an expensive solution to a phantom problem. Reject Prop. 39.
Manufactured crisis
Multiple groups have studied the issue and found scant evidence of widespread fraud. The California State Library (https://www.library.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/crb-reports/CRB-Voter-Fraud-Presentation-Senate-Elections-2026-04-03.pdf) looked at 14 counties where grand juries issued reports on the risk of voter fraud in the 2020, 2022 and 2024 elections and found secure elections everywhere. The Brennan Center for Justice’s research confirmed that voter fraud is a myth (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/debunking-voter-fraud-myth). Even the conservative Heritage Foundation could only find 71 instances (https://electionfraud.heritage.org/search?case_type=All&fraud_type=All&state=CA) of voter fraud in California — over more than four decades. Also, California already takes election integrity (https://abc7news.com/post/150000-mail-ballots-rejected-californias-primary-despite-efforts-count-every-vote/19571066/) seriously, which is one reason our process of confirming elections is so slow (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/17/upshot/california-slow-election-results.html).
RELATED: Endorsement Cheat Sheet: Mercury News and East Bay Times Editorial Boards’ top picks for California’s Nov. 3 general election (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/13/bay-area-news-group-california-election-endorsements-november-2026/)
Our editorial board repeatedly asked the Yes on Prop. 39 campaign for evidence of voter fraud in California, rampant or otherwise, and they deflected, dodged and denied the premise of our questions. They insisted that fraud wasn’t actually the issue — that Prop. 39 is about improving public trust and confidence in our democracy.
So it’s purely coincidence that Donald Trump demanded “voter ID” laws in California as a condition for wildfire disaster relief (https://abc7.com/post/president-donald-trump-wants-voter-id-laws-condition-aid-california/15833908/) last year. Or that the measure’s biggest backer, Illinois billionaire Richard Uihlein, has a history ofcontributing (https://www.propublica.org/article/uline-uihlein-election-denial) to the campaigns of election deniers.
According to the Public Policy Institute of California (https://data.ddhq.io/polls/2026/05/30/Public-Policy-Institute-of-California-California), a quarter of likely voters are very concerned that it’s too easy for ineligible people to vote. That’s not zero, but it also doesn’t mean we should be changing election laws to accommodate the fact-free fears of a minority of Californians.
In other polls about trust in our elections, it is overwhelmingly Republicans who are the most concerned. That’s fine. But if they really cared about improving those numbers, we’d recommend they start by asking the president to stop spreading false information.
We absolutely wouldn’t recommend, as Prop. 39 does, that private citizens be allowed to sue if they believe the government isn’t complying with the measure’s rules. We don’t even want to imagine the kind of frivolous litigation that could inspire.
Why panic?
It’s possible to view Prop. 39 and say, “What’s the big deal?” Thirty-six statesrequire (https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_identification_laws_by_state) voters to present identification before voting in person.
Well, the big deal is that a lot of eligible people might not be able to vote if the measure is passed. Millions of Californians (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/Who%20Lacks%20ID%20and%20Proof%20of%20Citizenship%20in%20California%20Today_.pdf) wouldn’t have the ID required to satisfy this proposal. (They’d have to request a new one.) And, as the No on Prop. 39 campaign pointed out to us, when Texas implemented similar mail-ballot ID rules, rejections shot up (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/) from 1% to 12%.
Plus, completely revamping the voter verification system will come with financial costs — “between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year,” according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Prop. 39 isn’t just about voter ID. It contains a provision that is deeply problematic: requiring election officials to use their “best efforts” to verify the citizenship status of voters they register, with regular audits to ensure compliance.
But there is no reliable government list of U.S. citizens. The Supreme Court decided that the federal government could continue to try to create one, but it’s already full of mistakes (https://www.npr.org/2026/09/25/nx-s1-5976804/supreme-court-trump-save-noncitizen-voting), labeling many citizens as ineligible to vote.
This deeply flawed measure would create chaos for no reason.
Reject Prop. 39.
(Editor’s note: To read our other recommendations for California’s Nov. 3 General Election, please visit mercurynews.com/endorsements (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/13/bay-area-news-group-california-election-endorsements-november-2026/).)
