I now have an extremely thorough picture. Let me summarize the key evidence:

**What Prop 39 does (from the actual constitutional text):**
1. Adds Art. II, §3.1 to the California Constitution.
2. Requires SOS and county officials to use "best efforts" to verify citizenship attestations using "government data" (both undefined), and report annually the % of each county's rolls that are citizenship-verified.
3. In-person voting: must present government-issued ID every time, in "any election in the State."
4. Mail voting: must write last 4 digits of a "unique identifying number" from a government-issued ID that MATCHES the one the voter designated in their registration. Officials "shall only count" a ballot after verifying identity.
5. Requires the state to provide a free voter ID card on request.
6. Self-executing; Legislature must "promptly enact" implementing laws; citizens may sue over compliance; State Auditor audits every odd-numbered year.
7. Severability.

**Key problems identified:**

A. **The advertised benefit isn't in the text.** The Yes campaign's core selling point is that a 4-digit PIN would *replace* unreliable signature verification, eliminating signature-mismatch rejections and speeding counting. But Prop 39 does NOT repeal Elections Code §3019 signature verification. The SOS's own "What your vote means" says a yes vote means voters "would be required to present **additional** identifying information." Common Cause, election-law experts, former Maricopa County Republican recorder Stephen Richer, Assembly Elections Committee chair Gail Pellerin (a former elections official), and Verified Voting all confirm it's additive. So mail voters get TWO independent ways to have a ballot rejected instead of one.

B. **No cure process.** Current law gives mail voters a robust notice-and-cure right for signature problems (Elections Code §3019(c)–(e); presumption the signature is valid; "an exact match is not required"; rejection only if two additional officials each find beyond a reasonable doubt that the signature differs in multiple, significant, and obvious respects; notice by mail + call/text/email; ~22 days to cure). Prop 39 contains **no** cure provision for the ID digits. The AG's official title says such ballots are "invalidated" — e.g., if you designated your SSN but write your DL number, your ballot doesn't count. Yet as recently as Nov 2, 2026, the Yes campaign told the East Bay Times the measure "allows a 'curring' process if a voter transposes numbers." That is not in the text. The SF Chronicle states flatly: "Prop 39 does not include a curing process for PIN codes."

C. **A factual claim in the official pro argument is false.** The pro argument says "In the last election, more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches." SOS data: 71,387 statewide for non-matching signatures in Nov 2024 (43,976 in June 2026). Total rejections of *all* kinds were 122,480 (0.9%). So the figure is overstated by ~40%, and Rivas/Limón specifically sought to strike it.

D. **Courts found the Yes campaign's ballot claims false.** Sacramento Superior Court Judge Shelleyanne Chang ruled the proponents' voter-guide claims that Prop 39 would "make voting easier," protect privacy, and "save millions of dollars" were false and misleading — "any statements that Proposition 39 will have an overall fiscal effect of saving *any* money... are objectively untrue" — and that it actually makes ID numbers "less private, and less secure." Proponents were forced to rewrite their argument. Separately, Judge Jennifer Rockwell upheld the AG's title ("Prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification") as accurate, rejecting the campaign's own claim that it wouldn't prevent anyone from voting — reasoning that "vote" plainly includes the tallying of a ballot. Two losses in one day, on the campaign's own litigation.

E. **Massive one-time re-registration burden.** The LAO confirms Prop 39 "requires new and existing voters to select a government-issued identification in their voter registration to vote by mail." The California Budget & Policy Center notes this "effectively means that people who are currently registered to vote would have to re-register." That's ~22–26 million registration records in a state where ~13 million of 16 million voters (over 80%) vote by mail. The AG's summary: "Prohibits voting by mail unless voter designates a government-issued identification number for their voter registration." Voters who miss this step may not receive a usable mail ballot at all.

F. **The citizenship-verification mandate is unworkable.** "Best efforts" and "government data" are undefined. There is no comprehensive federal database of U.S. citizens — federal systems track immigration status of foreign-born people, not the birthright citizenship of the ~90% of Americans born here. This is precisely why E-Verify has been resisted and why courts have repeatedly blocked similar mandates. Even the *San Diego Union-Tribune* — in DeMaio's own home region, and a paper that says "what's the big deal?" about in-person voter ID in 36 states — recommends NO on this ground alone: "the records needed to do it accurately don't exist." Risk: eligible citizens wrongly flagged and purged.

G. **The "free" ID isn't free, and millions lack qualifying ID.** A 2026 University of Maryland analysis found ~2.7 million Californians (11% of eligible voters) have no driver's license; another 13% have one that's expired or has an outdated address/name; 24% have no passport; 3+ million voting-age Californians would struggle to readily produce citizenship documents. People of color, young people, disabled Californians, low-income residents, and married women who changed their names are overrepresented. Real costs: travel, time off work, childcare, underlying documents.

H. **Privacy.** Last four digits of a government ID number — potentially an SSN — handwritten on the *outside* of an envelope alongside name, address and signature, then handled through the mail, drop boxes, poll workers, and ballot-processing vendors. California law (Gov. Code §7924.000) currently makes DL/ID/SSN numbers on registration affidavits confidential and non-disclosable. A judge already found the Yes campaign's privacy claim false, writing that Prop 39 "makes voter's 'government-issued identification' numbers less private, and less secure." The California Medical Association opposes partly on identity-theft grounds. Even libertarian *Reason*, which is sympathetic to voter ID, flags "an additional opportunity for identity theft."

I. **Litigation trap.** The measure is self-executing but leaves its core terms undefined, and grants *any citizen* a private right of action to sue the state or any of 58 counties over compliance. Loyola election-law professor Justin Levitt called it a "generic litigation trap." The SF Chronicle's framing: "CEQA for voting rights" — a never-ending lawsuit machine around every election, with results certified under legal cloud. The OC Register (pro-Yes) concedes: "we expect legal fights over the proposition as a whole and an adjustment period."

J. **It would slow counting, not speed it.** Experts across the spectrum (including Republican Stephen Richer) agree. Handwritten digits on 13 million envelopes must be read and matched, requiring scanning infrastructure counties don't have; county registrars told ABC7 that checking partial ID numbers could take longer than signature checks.

K. **The problem it solves is essentially nonexistent in California.** The California State Library's research bureau reviewed grand jury reports from 14 counties covering 2020–2024 and found "no evidence of systemic or significant fraud." The Heritage Foundation — the conservative think tank behind Project 2025 — documents just 71 voter-fraud cases in California across 1982–2025, all prosecuted. Brookings: "no election outcome in the US has ever been altered by ballot fraud." Brennan Center: impersonation fraud is rarer than being struck by lightning. Cato (libertarian): no good evidence noncitizens voted in detectable numbers in 2020. Noncitizen voting: ~30 referrals across 42 jurisdictions in 2016 = 0.0001% of votes cast. And notably, when the Mercury News editorial board repeatedly asked the Yes campaign for evidence of fraud, "they deflected, dodged and denied the premise" — insisting it's really about trust.

L. **The "trust" rationale is not supported by evidence.** PPIC data cited by the pro-side actually shows confidence in how California counts votes *rose* from 47%→63% (likely voters) between 2017 and 2024. Academic research (Persily, Stanford Law Review; UC Riverside/Western Washington studies in Political Research Quarterly and PS) finds strict voter ID laws have little to no effect on voter confidence — because confidence is driven by partisanship and whether your candidate won. So the measure is unlikely to deliver its stated benefit.

M. **The Texas cautionary precedent.** After Texas's 2021 mail-ballot ID law, rejection rates jumped from under 1% to over 12% — roughly 1 in 8 votes cast in the 2022 primary invalidated — and a peer-reviewed study (Journal of Politics / U. Chicago Press) found it reduced turnout in subsequent elections. The rebuttal in the voter guide cites "12 times more mail ballots" thrown out. California's baseline rejection rate is ~0.9%; even a modest increase in rejections would dwarf the fraud being prevented.

N. **The "bipartisan" framing doesn't hold up.** Yes money: $36.5M, of which Richard Uihlein (Wisconsin, Uline) gave $17M = 51.6% and Joseph Gebbia $8M = 24.3% — two donors = ~76%. **80.3% of Yes committee money came from outside California.** Every major political endorser is Republican (CA GOP, Steve Hilton, Ken Calvert, Tony Strickland, Bill Essayli). PPIC: 85% of Republicans support, 19% of Democrats. Citrin/Politico: 92% of Republicans yes, 80% of Democrats no; independents only 45–41. The campaign committee is run by Julie Luckey, mother of Trump megadonor Palmer Luckey. So while the *concept* of voter ID polls well in the abstract, the actual measure is a heavily out-of-state-funded Republican project — and support collapses once voters learn the details (it led or was close in early/September polls from SurveyUSA and Mason-Dixon, then fell to 37–41% yes in the final PPIC, Berkeley IGS, and Citrin/Politico polls as information spread).

O. **Editorial consensus against.** NO: SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee/McClatchy, San Diego Union-Tribune, Mercury News/East Bay Times/Bay Area News Group, Santa Cruz Sentinel. YES: OC Register, LA Daily News. That's 5 major boards to 2 — and notably the U-T is in the author's own district. The California Medical Association, ACLU, Common Cause, League of Women Voters, CA Democratic Party, CA Labor Federation, UCLA Voting Rights Project all oppose. Support: CA Republican Party, Reform California, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn, Uihlein.

**The strongest case for YES** (steelmanned fairly):
- Voter ID is genuinely popular in the abstract and exists in 36 states, plus Canada and Mexico. It's not inherently extremist.
- California does verify identity only by signature for 80%+ of voters, and signature matching is applied inconsistently across 58 counties; a 2022 Transparency Foundation report documented inconsistency.
- California's voter rolls do contain stale/inactive records, and ballots are mailed to addresses where people no longer live; ballot harvesting creates real abuse potential.
- The ID is free, and mail voting/extended hours are preserved.
- A former Secretary of State (Bill Jones, Republican) supports it.
- ~41–43% of Californians are genuinely concerned it's too easy for ineligible people to vote; that concern deserves a response.
- Research (NBER 2019 review; Research & Politics Dec 2024) finds strict ID laws have minimal aggregate turnout effects — so the suppression risk may be overstated in the aggregate.

**Why that case still doesn't carry the day here:**
The generic voter-ID argument is not what's on the ballot. ## My answer: **NO**

I read the actual constitutional text, the Legislative Analyst's fiscal estimate, the Attorney General's title and summary, the ballot arguments, both court rulings, the campaign finance filings, the Secretary of State's ballot-rejection data, and the editorial positions across the state. Here's why I land on no.

---

### What's actually in the text (Art. II, §3.1)

- In-person: show government-issued ID **every time**, in "any election in the State."
- By mail: handwrite the last four digits of a designated government ID number on the envelope. Officials "shall only count" the ballot after verifying identity.
- Officials must use "best efforts" to verify citizenship using "government data" — **both terms undefined**.
- Free state voter ID card on request; State Auditor compliance audits in odd years; **any citizen may sue** the state or any county over compliance; declared "self-executing."

### The five findings that decided this for me

**1. The main benefit being advertised is not in the measure.** DeMaio and the Yes campaign say the four-digit PIN *replaces* signature matching. It doesn't — Prop 39 never repeals Elections Code §3019. The Secretary of State's own guide says a yes vote means voters provide "**additional** identifying information." Common Cause, Loyola election-law scholars, former Maricopa County recorder Stephen Richer (R), Assembly Elections Chair Gail Pellerin (a former registrar), and Verified Voting all agree: mail voters get **two** independent ways to be rejected instead of one. Even *Reason*, which is sympathetic to voter ID, says it would "no doubt burden our excruciatingly slow ballot counting."

**2. There is no cure process — for a brand-new failure point.** Today, a signature problem triggers a strong statutory safety net: a presumption your signature is valid, "an exact match is not required," rejection only if two extra officials each find a mismatch "beyond a reasonable doubt," notice by mail plus call/text/email, and ~22 days to fix it. Prop 39 has **no cure provision at all**. The AG's official summary says the ballot is simply "invalidated" — write your driver's license number when you designated your SSN and your vote doesn't count. Yet on Nov. 2 the Yes campaign told the East Bay Times it "allows a 'curring' process if a voter transposes numbers." That promise exists only in a press quote, not in the constitution they're asking you to ratify. Texas is the cautionary case: after its 2021 mail-ballot ID law, rejections went from under 1% to **over 12%** — roughly 1 in 8 votes invalidated — and a peer-reviewed study found turnout fell.

**3. The pro argument's central statistic is false, and a judge already ruled against this campaign twice.** The ballot argument claims "more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches" in the last election. SOS data: **71,387** statewide in Nov. 2024 (43,976 in June 2026). Separately, Judge Shelleyanne Chang found the proponents' claims that Prop 39 makes voting "easier," protects privacy, and "saves millions" to be **false and misleading** — writing that the measure actually makes ID numbers "less private, and less secure," and that savings claims were "objectively untrue." They were forced to rewrite their argument. Judge Jennifer Rockwell then upheld the AG's title — "**Prohibits** citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification" — rejecting the campaign's own insistence that it bars nobody from voting, because "vote" plainly includes the counting. When a measure's sponsors lose both of their own lawsuits over how it's described, that's information.

**4. The citizenship-verification mandate can't be executed.** There is no comprehensive government list of U.S. citizens. Federal databases track the immigration status of the foreign-born — not the birthright citizenship of the ~90% of Americans born here. That's why E-Verify has been resisted for decades and why courts have repeatedly blocked comparable mandates. The risk runs at eligible citizens being wrongly flagged and purged. Notably, the **San Diego Union-Tribune** — in DeMaio's own region, and a board that says "what's the big deal?" about in-person ID in 36 other states — still recommends no on this ground alone: "the records needed to do it accurately don't exist."

**5. The problem is tiny; the exposure is enormous.** The California State Library reviewed grand jury reports from 14 counties covering 2020–2024 and found **no evidence of systemic or significant fraud**. The Heritage Foundation — the conservative think tank behind Project 2025 — documents just **71** California voter-fraud cases across 1982–2025, all prosecuted. Brookings: "no election outcome in the US has ever been altered by ballot fraud." Against that: 13 million mail ballots per presidential cycle and roughly **22 million existing registrants** who would each have to affirmatively re-designate an ID (the LAO confirms this applies to "new and existing voters"; the Budget & Policy Center says it "effectively means" re-registering) in a state where 80%+ vote by mail. A 2026 University of Maryland analysis found ~2.7 million Californians (11% of eligible voters) have no driver's license, another 13% hold one that's expired or has a stale address or name, and 3+ million would struggle to produce citizenship documents — with people of color, young, disabled, low-income, and married women who changed names overrepresented. And you'd be writing the last four of a government ID — possibly an SSN — on the *outside* of an envelope next to your name, address, and signature, when Gov. Code §7924.000 currently keeps those numbers strictly confidential.

### The strongest case for yes, and why it falls short

It's real and I don't want to strawman it. Voter ID is popular in the abstract; 36 states have some form, as do Canada and Mexico. California verifies 80%+ of voters by handwriting judgment applied unevenly across 58 counties. Our rolls do carry stale records, ballots do get mailed to people who've moved, and ballot harvesting has genuine abuse potential. The ID is free, mail voting and extended hours survive, and a former Republican Secretary of State, Bill Jones, supports it. Aggregate research (a 2019 NBER review; *Research & Politics*, Dec. 2024) finds strict ID laws have minimal net turnout effects.

But none of that rescues **this drafting**. Add a private right of action letting anyone sue any of 58 counties over undefined compliance duties and you get what Loyola's Justin Levitt called a "generic litigation trap" and the Chronicle called "CEQA for voting rights" — permanent litigation cloud over every result. Put it in the constitution as self-executing with the operative terms blank, and the errors are much harder to fix than a statute's: correcting them later takes another statewide vote or a two-thirds legislative amendment that "furthers the purposes of the act." The LAO prices it at tens of millions to low hundreds of millions **every year**. And the "bipartisan" framing doesn't survive the finance reports: Richard Uihlein of Wisconsin gave $17M (51.6%) and Joseph Gebbia $8M (24.3%) — two donors, ~76% of the money — with **80.3% of Yes funds from outside California**, and every major political endorser a Republican. PPIC found 85% of Republicans and 19% of Democrats in favor. The measure polled competitively in September, then fell to 37–41% yes in the final PPIC, Berkeley IGS, and Citrin/Politico surveys as voters learned the details — which is what you'd expect when the specifics are worse than the slogan.

Finally, the trust rationale is undercut by the proponents' own data: PPIC shows confidence in how California counts votes **rose** from 47% to 63% among likely voters between 2017 and 2024. And multiple studies find strict ID laws barely move voter confidence, because confidence tracks partisanship and whether your candidate won. When the Mercury News board repeatedly asked the Yes campaign for evidence of fraud, they report the campaign "deflected, dodged and denied the premise."

Editorial boards: **No** — SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee/McClatchy, San Diego Union-Tribune, Mercury News/East Bay Times, Santa Cruz Sentinel. **Yes** — OC Register, LA Daily News. Opposed by the CMA, ACLU, Common Cause, League of Women Voters, and the UCLA Voting Rights Project.

**Vote no.** If you want election-integrity reform, the durable route is statutory: fund county election offices, let counties join the multistate voter-roll accuracy consortium they've been requesting, tighten who may collect ballots, and require counting to begin the day ballots are mailed. That addresses the legitimate concerns without entrenching an undefined, cure-less mandate in the state constitution.
